en: (1) The members of a compound are separated by periods. (2) External sandhi is decomposed with `^`. (3) Verbs are marked by `(`.
[The Glorious Smṛti of Bṛhaspati] In former times, men were devoted to dharma and were non-violent;
however, for those overcome by greed and hatred, legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) was introduced.
If the master does not pay wages to servants who are performing their work, and if the servants do not perform it, then a legal dispute arises in that matter.
For someone may commit violence, or one may fail to pay what is due;
these two are the grounds for dispute, and between them, the latter has more frequent occurrence.
When property is sold and money is taken for the purpose of a debt,
that value, together with the principal debt, is known as *vyavahāra* (legal transaction).
[1.1.1 Qualities of a King] Therefore, I shall describe in due order the duties pertaining to the qualities of a king:
creditors, debtors, disputes, sureties, documents, and witnesses.
Listen to the origin of him who correctly investigates [the self],
as well as that of Soma, Agni, Arka, Anila, Indra, Vitta, Āpatti, and Yama.
Having extracted the mere essence of fire, the form of the King was indeed fashioned;
all beings, both moving and stationary, are composed of that.

Out of fear [of punishment], people are able to enjoy their wealth and do not deviate from their own duties; in a kingless state, there is no cultivation, trade, lending at interest, or protection of property.
Therefore, he was created of old as the leader of the social classes and stages of life;
legal procedure (vyavahāra) consists of two parts, arising from property and injury.
The root of wealth consists of fourteen [factors], while the root of violence is fourfold:
two types of harshness, killing, and likewise the abduction of another's wife.
Lending at interest, finding hidden treasure, partnership in business, failure to pay wages, non-service, false claims regarding land, and selling what one does not own; 1.1.011a-b.
Rescission of purchase and sale, breach of contract,
the union of man and woman, theft, partition of inheritance, and gambling with dice.
These fourteen words, which originate from [the four] meanings,
are further divided in this way into many tens by means of the distinctions in action.
Bṛhaspati has stated that there are four categories arising from injury: the two types of verbal abuse, assault, and likewise the abduction of another's wife.
They are distinguished separately according to whether they are inferior, middling, or superior; the specific distinction among these four is likewise set forth in their proper order.
These eighteen topics are declared in the treatises on Dharma;
those who know them to be the foundation of all disputes are the true investigators.

The first quarter is known as the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the second likewise as the rejoinder (*uttara*), the third quarter should be stated as the application (*kriyāpāda*), and the fourth is the final determination (*nirṇaya*).

[1.1.3 The Strength and Weakness of the Fourfold Authority: Dharma, etc. Through *dharma*, through legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), through conduct (*cāritra*), and by the king’s command, the determination of a doubtful matter is declared to be fourfold.
Where a decision is made by relying solely upon the sacred scriptures (śāstra), that should be known as legal procedure (vyavahāra); through it, too, dharma increases.
When a decision is made based on local custom, inference,
and the consensus of merchants, the legal proceeding itself is subverted.
Where a king, setting aside established custom and conduct, makes a decision, that indeed is the royal command; by it, established conduct is superseded.

In accordance with the treatises on Dharma, the king— accompanied by his ministers and his domestic priest, free from anger and greed, truthful, and having conquered his senses— should examine legal cases for the sake of protecting his subjects.
[1.1.4 The Section on Dharma] That which consists of seven constituent elements for both the seeker of victory and the enemy—
this is indeed declared to be the fourteen-fold circle (*maṇḍala*).
There are four protectors of the earth, and together with their separate allies, they constitute eight.
And these, along with ministers and others, are imperishably united in this world.
Having risen in the morning and performed purification according to the rules,
the king [should honor] his gurus, astrologers, physicians, gods, Brahmins, and domestic priests.
Having honored these [elders] as is appropriate with fine flowers, ornaments, and garments,
and having greeted his teachers and others with a cheerful countenance, he should enter the assembly hall.
The king, surrounded by three virtuous men, should examine the legal cases after entering the excellent assembly hall, whether seated or standing.
[1.1.5 Characteristics of a Fort] For the protection of his own person, his wives, his wealth, and his subjects— which have been accumulated—
the king should cause a fort to be constructed, provided with two types of walls.

It should be provided with the fuel and liquids for kings, such as cane, young grass, food, and vehicles, as well as various machines, weapons, and materials, and accompanied by affectionate and heroic men.
Having summoned Brahmins learned in the Vedas and Kṣatriyas who maintain the sacred fire-offerings,
he should establish them there and provide for their livelihood.
Taxes shall not be levied upon them; houses and lands should be granted to them, and they should be made exempt from the king's authority by recording this in his own edict.

They shall perform the daily rites (*nitya*), the occasional rites (*naimittika*), the rites for desired ends (*kāmya*), as well as those for pacification (*śāntika*) and prosperity (*pauṣṭika*); likewise, they shall carry out the ancient rituals (*paurāṇa-karman*) and the administration of doubtful cases.
Wherever the ground is level or even uneven, in whatever manner it may be,
the halls, towers, moats, and other such structures should be constructed accordingly.
Thereafter, the subjects— namely the twice-born, Vaiśyas, merchants, artisans, craftsmen, and guards— should construct their dwellings all around that [central area].
He shall establish barracks, standing enclosures, places for removal, roundabouts, pits, crossroads, as well as assembly grounds, marketplaces, and cow-pens.
How can one who has been proclaimed as "virtuous" in the assembly of people be described as "devoid of virtue" by that very same mouth?
Therefore, one should not deprive an innocent person of his authority or livelihood;
otherwise, there would be the consequence of endless instability, and his protection would perish.
But having properly settled the territory and constructed a fortress according to the treatises,
he should constantly apply his supreme effort to the removal of thorns.
That protection of the subjects has been declared by those who know the law to be threefold:
[protection] from foreign armies, from the fear of thieves, and from the powerful who act unjustly.
The king should pacify the fear of thieves from enemy armies through strategic means; and for those oppressed by the powerful, he should provide daily adjudication of justice.
Whatever one studies, whatever one sacrifices, whatever one offers oblations, and whatever one worships—
the king becomes entitled to a sixth part of that through his proper protection.
Protecting all beings according to dharma and executing those deserving of death, the king performs sacrifices day after day with fees of a hundred thousand.
A cultivator shall pay a tenth, an eighth, or a sixth part as tax to the king,
respectively, from fallow land, from land sown in the rainy season, and from land sown in the spring.
According to local custom, they shall pay tribute—whether monthly, half-yearly, or annually;
this is declared to be the ancient law for cultivators.

[1.1.7 The Manner of Constructing the Assembly Hall] In the center of the fort, one should build a separate residence— whether it be water-based, mountain-based, arboreal, marshy, or desert-based— surrounded by water and trees.
To the east of that [hall], one should construct an auspicious assembly hall facing the east,
provided with garlands, incense, and seats, and furnished with seeds and gems.

It should be provided with images, paintings, and deities, as well as with fire and water; it should be auspiciously marked and endowed with the characteristics described in the treatises on architecture.
Having occupied the auspicious throne, with his limbs properly covered and his mind composed,
he should pay homage to the guardians of the world and then begin the inspection of affairs.
The Brahmin is the root of the tree of Dharma; the king is its trunk and branches; the ministers are its leaves and flowers; and protection by means of justice is its fruit.
Fame, wealth, the essence of fruits, enjoyment, acquisition of attendants, honor, invincibility, inclusion in the ranks of the world, and an eternal station in heaven.
Having drunk these juices of justice, and having become impartial toward the dispute,
the king— having abandoned greed and other such vices— should carry out the legal determination in accordance with Dharma.
The king himself should preside over disputes concerning livelihoods;
he is served by the learned according to the path seen in the scriptures.
Therefore, a king should protect [his subjects] properly and with diligent effort according to justice;
from that, he shall obtain wealth, sovereignty, and vast fame.
The gods know truth in brief, while humans know falsehood;
he whose mind is established in truth attains divinity even in this very world.
The sacrifice arises from the conjunction of the animal, the clarified butter, the officiating priests, and so forth;
just as it is connected with these, so is its conventional designation explained.

But he who, among the chief judge and the members of the court, reaches a decision on matters of law by relying on their opinions through the application of logical reasoning, does not deserve punishment.

[1.1.8 Classifications of Assemblies] The assembly is declared to be of four kinds: established, unestablished, sealed, and likewise disciplined; and the members of the assembly are of the same types.
In a city it is established, while in a village it is called "mobile" (calā) because it is not established;
it is sealed, associated with a superintendent, connected to the king, and governed.
One who, having formed a firm resolve, examines legal cases— that assembly is equal to a sacrificial rite.
The members of the assembly (*sabhya*) should be seven, five, or even three, being experts in worldly affairs, the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and the Dharma.
That assembly hall where the foremost of Brahmins are seated is equal to a sacrifice.
The king should always keep the plaintiff and the defendant under guard without requiring sureties;
that court of justice (*karaṇa*) which consists of these ten components is the one in which the monarch should reside.
Having set aside one-eighth part of the day, one should rest well;
that time is declared in the scriptures as the supreme period for legal proceedings.
The king should appoint as members of the court those who are engaged in performing virtuous deeds, devoted to truth and righteousness, free from anger and greed, and learned in the scriptures.
There should be seven, five, or three members of the court assembly;
those who are ignorant of local customs, atheists, or devoid of scriptural knowledge [should not be included].
Those who are insane, angry, greedy, or afflicted by pain should not be questioned in a legal determination.

The king, or else a learned Brahmin acting as the chief justice, shall examine the legal cases, having placed at the forefront the constituent elements of justice and remaining steadfast in the opinion of the court members and the sacred scriptures.
Because he delights the subjects by means of the fourfold power (*caturaṅga-bala*),
and because he shines with his own physical form, he is therefore called a "king" (*rājā*). However,
this single term has been declared by the wise to have many applications in common usage.
The king and the learned Brahmin are the final arbiters of that [dispute].
The Vedic scripture states that he who asks the question concerning the matter relied upon in legal proceedings is called *prāṭ*; and he who disputes therein is traditionally known as *prāḍvivāka*.
In a legal dispute, he asks the question and likewise the counter-question;
because he speaks first with kind words, he is therefore known as the *prāḍvivāka*.

The king who presides over the court together with the judge, the ministers, the Brahmin domestic priest, and the members of the assembly, remains in heaven by virtue of his righteousness as an impartial observer.

He should appoint as a minister a twice-born Brāhmaṇa who knows the meaning of all the scriptures, is free from greed, speaks with justice, is wise, and has attained his position through successive steps.
He who overlooks legal matters while excluding the twice-born and instead deals with them alongside the Śūdras,
his kingdom flows away and his army and treasury perish.
And for those who roam the forest, their trial shall take place in the forest;
likewise, for soldiers it shall be in the army, and for merchants in the caravans.
Plowmen, artisans, wrestlers, those who live by usury, guilds, mendicants, and thieves— their legal determination shall be according to their own specific laws.
Families, guilds, and assemblies—the king is the authority over these; they are the foundations of legal proceedings, each succeeding one being more authoritative than the preceding.
But the affairs of ascetics he should have carried out by those learned in the three Vedas alone,
and likewise by those who know the application of *māyā*, and never by himself for fear of provoking anger.
A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it,
incurs great infamy and goes to hell.
Whether it be a brother, a son, a worthy guest, a father-in-law, or even a maternal uncle—
if he has deviated from his own duty, there is no one who is exempt from punishment by the king.
Where there is no learned Brahmin, one should appoint a Kṣatriya there, or a Vaiśya who knows the treatises on Dharma; one should avoid a Śūdra with every effort.
But he who is devoid of righteous conduct and actions, though possessing the external marks of a Brahmin,
yet claims "I am a Brahmin"— him they call a *brāhmaṇabruva* (one who merely calls himself a Brahmin).
The king should appoint as accountants and scribes those who know the true nature of words and their designations, who are skilled in calculation, pure, and not ignorant of scripts.
When witnesses, the plaintiff, or the defendant fail to appear without a valid reason, that man who speaks the truth must be appointed by the members of the court as the guardian of the case.
That assembly in which a king, having seated himself, observes justice with a disciplined mind by means of these ten constituent parts, is equal to a sacrificial rite.
Among these limbs, the king is declared to be the head and the mouth; the members of the court are the arms, the legal codes are the hands, and the calculator and the scribe are the shanks.
Gold, fire, water, and spies, as well as the heart, the feet, and one's own men.
The king should place gold, fire, water, the treatises on Dharma, as well as sacred objects and things beneficial to the people in their midst.
One should visualize the Sun, the Moon, the gods and others, as well as the guardians of the directions there;
indeed, gold, fire, water, and one's own person are the ten constituent means.
The duties of all these ten individuals have been declared separately:
the speaker, the presiding officer, the king, the punisher, and the member who examines the case.

Smṛti declares that the decision [of the court] shall consist of the awarding of victory, as well as punishment; furthermore, for the purpose of an oath, gold, fire, and water are used when the persons concerned are thirsty.
The accountant shall calculate the matter; the scribe shall record the legal argument;
and his own attendants shall summon the parties, the petitioners, the members of the court, and the witnesses.

The punishment of speech and the punishment of censure are both dependent upon the Brahmin; however, the punishment of fines and corporal punishment are both said to be under the authority of the king.
Those families, guilds, corporations, and so forth, who are properly known by the king,
shall perform the legal affairs of men, excluding cases involving violence and injustice.
The heads of families, guilds, and assemblies are declared to be the makers of legal decisions;
a case that has not been deliberated upon by families should be deliberated upon by guilds.
What is not known by the guilds (gaṇa) is known by the corporations (śreṇī); what is not known by the corporations is known by the appointed officials (niyuktaka).
The members of the court (sabhyāḥ) have authority over the families and other such groups; the superintendent (adhyakṣa) is declared to have authority over them.
The king is superior to all because he diligently adjudicates disputes among those who are highest, lowest, and middling, thereby determining the Dharma.
The cognitions of the Lord move ever higher above all other cognitions [those of those] who are beset by the darkness of ignorance and covered by the film of doubt.
He who renders the scriptures free from defects by means of the probe of scriptural collyrium attains fame in this world, honor from kings, and a destination in heaven.

He who, having abandoned greed, hatred, and the like, should carry out the determination of legal affairs according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice.
But the members of the court shall not neglect a case that has proceeded contrary to dharma; by neglecting it, those kings go headlong to hell.
But having recognized that the mind of the king has strayed from the path of justice, one should speak what is unpleasant there; a member of the assembly does not thereby become a sinner.
First, the member of the court must speak words consistent with dharma and artha;
if the king does not listen, then that member of the court remains blameless.
If the judge should converse in secret with a litigant regarding a matter that has not yet been determined,
he too shall be punished, as shall the members of the court, especially so.
Whether through ignorance, delusion, greed, or even malice,
where a member of the assembly speaks falsely, he is considered an unseemly person and should be punished.
Where there is no document, no witness, and no possession, and where no means of proof exist, the king alone is the sole authority in that case.
Those discourses which cannot be determined and whose nature is doubtful—
the king shall be the authority for them, since he is the lord of all.
Every day, surrounded by his courtiers, he should personally oversee legal proceedings.
Those courtiers who speak unjustly, as well as those who live by taking bribes,
and those who deceive the person who trusts them— all of these must be banished.
Whether appointed or unappointed, one who knows the treatises is qualified to speak; whatever he declares in that assembly is the Dharma—of this there is no doubt.
The king should sit facing the east, while the members of the court face the north;
the calculator faces the west, and the scribe faces the south.
Just as Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when the appointed time arrives, so too must subjects be restrained by the king; for that indeed is the vow of Yama.
In accordance with the *Dharmaśāstra* and the *Arthaśāstra*, the king,
examining the course of legal proceedings with skill, should administer justice.
If, however, the members of the court decide here by overstepping the treatises on logic (*nyāyaśāstra*), then dharma is destroyed; it destroys everyone without a doubt.
The treatises of Manu and others are to be upheld, and never the treatises on worldly affairs (*artha-śāstra*).
When there is a conflict between the two, one must act according to the words proclaimed in the *dharma-śāstra*.
A definitive conclusion should not be reached by relying on the scriptures alone;
for if an inquiry is devoid of reason, the loss of Dharma arises.
Having occupied that [throne] in the forenoon, he should look upon [his affairs] with aged ministers and dependents,
and likewise listen to the ancient treatises on dharma and artha.
Through worldly convention, a thief may become a non-thief, and a virtuous person an unvirtuous one;
without logical investigation, Māṇḍavya was treated as a thief.
Unreal things appear like real ones, and real things appear like unreal ones;
since they are seen to produce delusion, one should investigate them through reasoning.
In sacrifice Viṣṇu is worshipped; in legal procedure the lord of the earth is worshipped. Here, the victor is the sacrificer, while the defeated is declared to be the sacrificial victim.

The first and second parts [of the lawsuit] are known as the plaintiff's and the defendant's positions; the three Vedas and the legal treatises are the sacrificial fires; the members of the court are the officiating priests; and self-restraint is the sacrificial fee.
In the same way, the calculator and the scribe should be understood as the two witnesses;
this judicial proceeding has been declared to be equal to a sacrificial rite.

When one, unassailed by others, brings a matter before the king by a path that deviates from the traditional law (*smṛti*) and established custom (*ācāra*), that indeed constitutes a subject for legal dispute.
A plaint brought by one who is an outcaste or the like, by one who has not returned to his natural state,
or by one acting without independence, does not succeed.
A legal proceeding initiated by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted, suffering from a calamity, a child, or an elderly person,
as well as one conducted by an unrelated party, is not valid.
A teacher and a pupil, father and son, husband and wife, and master and servant— among these, when they are joined together, no legal transaction is valid.
In this manner, the judge should cause the plaintiff's case, as examined by the members of the court, to be recorded in writing;
however, he shall not investigate a dispute that is not well-known or one that is offensive to the people.

[1.1.10 The laws of place and caste must likewise be protected: "The laws that have been established for those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*), as well as for those dwelling in difficult terrains, and for the customs of regions, castes, families, and so forth— these must be maintained."
In that very same way, those subjects must be protected; otherwise, they become agitated. When the people are alienated, the army and the treasury perish.
In the South, twice-born men marry the daughters of their maternal uncles;
in the Middle Country, laborers and artisans eat beef.
In the east, men were fish-eaters and women were devoted to sexual misconduct;
in the north, women drank liquor and menstruating women were touchable by men.
Those born of the same womb take the wife of their brother who is without a husband;
by this act, they do not become liable to penance or punishment.
Because they constantly fail to perform what is enjoined and because they indulge in what is forbidden,
the king, having provided them with food and clothing, shall take the remainder of their produce.

[The offspring of those born in the inverse order, as well as those dwelling in difficult regions, must be protected with effort according to the scriptures; for when there is doubt, she is the means of proof.]
Having observed that [custom], one should make a decision according to the established order previously settled for the assembly hall,
the customary tolls, fines, and the monthly or half-monthly taxes.
A boundary should always be established in writing and supervised by merchants;
the claim of the plaintiff must be acted upon, as must the claim of the defendant.
Having examined the matter, one should take a step [to act]; otherwise, one shall go to hell.
A lawsuit between one person and many others, or against women, or against spectators,
is declared by those who know the Dharma to be inadmissible.

[1.1.11 Those Who Should Not Be Imprisoned] One engaged in a sacrificial session (sattra), one preparing for a wedding, the sick, those afflicted by grief, the insane, children, the intoxicated, the elderly, one who has been summoned for trial, one occupied with royal business, and one observing a vow.
A soldier on the battlefield, a cultivator during the harvest season, those in a precarious situation, and likewise women accompanied by a protector, must not be arrested when they are nearby.

A minor who has not yet attained legal capacity, a messenger, one intent on giving a gift, one observing a vow, those in a precarious situation, and likewise women who have a protector, shall not be obstructed.
But when grain has grown, the farmer who has sold his crop to a merchant,
as well as those who have set up a public storehouse (satra) and those who have undertaken a commercial enterprise, should be made to pay once their transactions are completed.
When the mind is unable to resolve a dispute even though one desires to engage in it, time for deliberation should be granted to both the plaintiff and the defendant.
Whether the accuser brings a charge based on truth or even out of suspicion,
the king shall cause that very person to be summoned by means of a female slave or a male servant.
In the case of those who are timid, dull-witted, insane, aged, female, minor, or diseased, a kinsman,
or another person appointed by the court, shall state both the preceding and the subsequent [evidence].
In the case of a sacrificial priest and a litigant, when both are equally engaged, they are declared to be equal;
in the sacrifice, the patron obtains merit, whereas in the legal dispute, he obtains either loss or victory.
If one who has been summoned does not come out of arrogance, even though supported by the strength of his kinsmen,
the judge shall impose upon him a fine proportionate to the nature of the legal claim.
At the appropriate time, he should question the one who has come for business while he stands before him with a bowed head:
"What is your business? What is your distress? Do not fear; speak, O man."

When he has been questioned in this manner, whatever he may say, the members of the court, together with the Brahmins, should deliberate upon it; if the matter is found to be just, then further steps for his summons shall follow.
He should provide a seal, or he may direct that a document or a person be sent [as a substitute].
But if one who has been summoned disregards the royal command while being capable of complying, the king shall determine his punishment in accordance with the nature of the accusation.
One should not employ those who are unskilled, children, the elderly, those in a precarious state, or those overwhelmed by other duties.
For minor offenses, the fine shall be fifty; for middling offenses, it shall be at least one hundred;
and for serious matters, the offender shall always be fined at least five hundred.
In a region destroyed by an enemy army, or afflicted by famine or disease,
one should issue a call for renewed recruitment but should not impose punishment.
[One should avoid those] occupied with the neglect of duties, those addicted to vices, those busy with the king's business, and those distracted by festivals.

The king should not summon servants who are aged, those who have risen against him, those who are dependent on others, those of deceitful character, or those who are intoxicated, insane, or negligent.
Neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor one acting under a mandate,
shall be liable to punishment when speaking falsely for the sake of another in legal proceedings.

A young woman born of a noble family who has not yet reached her menses, a woman who has recently given birth, and a maiden who is the most excellent among all castes— these are declared by the wise to be "enjoyed" by their paternal kinsmen.

Having ascertained the time and place, as well as the relative strength and weakness of the cases, the king should gradually cause even those who are incapable of traveling to appear by means of vehicles.

The summoning of those who are dependent on others for their livelihood, of women who live by their own will, of courtesans, of those who have lost their family status, and of those who are outcasts is prescribed.
A surety capable of resolving the legal matter should be accepted from both parties.
Even those such as forest-dwellers who have renounced the world, once their intent is known,
the king should cause them to be summoned for important matters, provided he does not provoke their anger.
While the matter is yet to be stated, the plaintiff shall restrain the defendant from departing, whether he stands still or moves away,
until the appearance for summons has been made.

Restriction from staying in place, restriction by time, restriction from travel, and likewise restriction from work—restriction is of these four kinds; one who is under restriction must not violate it.
Fields, gardens, houses, and the like, as well as wealth, grain, and so forth—
these are to be subject to legal restraint for litigants who speak unrighteously.
But if one who has been placed under restraint should himself voluntarily relinquish that restraint,
there is no fault on account of his transgression, nor shall a fine be imposed upon him.
After reporting to the king, the person who has placed a blockade shall not lift it on his own;
if he should lift it, he shall be made to pay a fine, and one who has been blockaded shall not violate the restriction.
In cases such as crossing a river, traversing a wilderness, or encountering danger in difficult terrain,
one who departs in order to avoid an unfulfilled prohibition does not commit an offense.

One who desires to marry, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to sacrifice, one beset by calamity, one attacked by another, and likewise one engaged in the king's business— [these are exempt from being summoned].
Cowherds [must attend] when cattle are grazing; farmers, when the crops are beginning to grow; artisans, at their respective times; and soldiers, during times of conflict.
Those who have climbed a tree or a mountain, those standing on elephants, horses, chariots, or boats,
and those situated in difficult terrain— all of them must not be obstructed by those seeking to accomplish their business.
But he who, by restraining his senses through fasting, breath-control, and so forth,
should cause [the debtor] to be restrained by means of restraints— he is not to be fined, for he has not transgressed.
One who is subject to restraint and yet evades it deserves punishment;
however, one who restrains a person who is not subject to restraint shall be punished by the king—this is the established rule.

The king should examine the legal pleadings of those who have come forward to dispute, even if they are litigants who have argued repeatedly; however, he should not consider pleadings drafted by himself nor those presented by his own officials.
[1.1.13 The Sequence of Speech for the Plaintiff and the Defendant] When one is oppressed, has come of his own accord, or seeks [redress] through legal means,
the judge— or a representative— should question him slowly and steadily.
The statement of one who acts without being authorized— because he is not permitted to engage in legal transactions—
is not to be accepted as evidence, except in the case of a written document or a message sent by him.
When the plaintiff and the defendant both arrive by claiming "I came first," the trial should be conducted according to the order of their castes, or else by considering whose suffering is greater.

Those who are insane, intoxicated, or driven away; those defiled by a heinous crime; and those who are mentally deficient, very old, or children—these should be known as those who cannot be held liable.

"A thesis that has been stated but is unacceptable, as well as a proponent who fails to provide a reply—such a proponent and such a thesis are not to be accepted; I shall now explain what kind of proponent and what kind of thesis are to be accepted."

When a proponent, intent on establishing his own position, speaks with the intention of expressing something by resorting to an exaggeration of the affliction [of the opponent], that is called the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie argument).
The *bhāṣā* stage, the *uttara* stage, likewise the *kriyā* stage, and the *pratyākalita* stage: legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) consists of these four stages.

"False confession (*mithyā-sampratipatti*), as well as counter-attack (*pratyavaskandana*), prior plea (*prāṅnyāya*)—these four replies have been declared by those who know the treatises. In the case of a false reply (*mithyā*), there are four parts; likewise in the case of a counter-attack."

In a case of prior litigation, that [defendant] is to be understood as being in the wrong when he fails to respond, even though he is being urged by various means during the proceedings. If, after seven nights have passed, he still does not provide an answer, he is defeated and deserves punishment.

[1.2.1 Definition of the Thesis] Once that [opponent] has been present, the proponent should formulate a thesis (pakṣa) that is faultless, accompanied by a proposition (pratijñā), and consistent with valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and authoritative tradition (āgama).
One should record the place, location, year, month, fortnight, day, name, and caste; as well as the substance, number, profit, injury, and the signs of emaciation.
Furthermore, one should not alter the nature of the matter for which one brings a lawsuit.
And he should not go to another side; by going [to another side], he is defeated from his previous position.
[1.2.2 Faults of the Thesis] The king should avoid a thesis that is unestablished, faulty, meaningless, purposeless, impossible to prove, or contradictory.
That which has not been composed by anyone is declared to be "unestablished" (*aprasiddha*).
That which has a different meaning and lacks its own intended meaning is proclaimed to be "defective" (*sadoṣa*).
One with a minor offense and a minor claim is known as "insignificant" (*nirarthaka*);
however, that which is devoid of any obstruction to the accomplishment of the task should be understood as "purposeless" (*niṣprayojana*).
A legal proceeding that is deficient in terms such as "idleness" and the like is considered futile;
likewise, one that involves verbal abuse, physical assault, and so forth should be understood as purposeless.
"‘This person must give me a bow made of hare’s horn’—
the wise call such a claim an impossible and unachievable plea.
When such a plea is presented before the judge and the king..."
When there is opposition within one's own kingdom, it is called "internal conflict" (*viruddha*).

Those who know the subject (*pakṣa*) declare that it is free from defects of the proposition, is something to be proven, is accompanied by valid reasons, is well-defined, and is established in the world.
It consists of very few syllables yet contains abundant meaning; it is free from ambiguity and confusion;
it is devoid of contradictory reasons and serves as a refutation of opposing views.
In legal proceedings, when disputants must speak without confusion, the statement itself constitutes the proposition (*pratijñā*), for its meaning is the subject (*pakṣa*).
Whether due to delusion or out of deceit, that which was not stated by the proponent—
whether it be included within the reply or otherwise— that too shall be accepted from both parties.

Having properly considered such qualities as these and being well-ascertained, a thesis (*pakṣa*) that has been formulated is acceptable; otherwise, it is a fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*). Furthermore, one that is devoid of place and time, or lacking in substance and number, is likewise unacceptable.
And a thesis that lacks both the probandum and the means of valid cognition is held to be unacceptable.
If a plaintiff records a plea that is based on falsehood, lacks logical connection or legal action, concerns an impossible matter, or is confused,
he suffers a loss of his suit.
If a litigant, having stated a charge, should overstep it and state another,
or having declared a line of action, should speak otherwise, that plaintiff shall suffer defeat.
In the first stage of the trial, the plaintiff shall rectify any deficiency or excess;
he shall not proceed to the next stage until the defendant has been confronted in the presence of the assessors.
In cases of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, or violating the teacher’s wife,
as well as in other instances of indecent speech, no counter-argument is permitted.
In the case of killing a human being, theft, violating another's wife,
eating forbidden food, and the abduction or defilement of a maiden;
In cases of verbal or physical assault, forgery, and likewise treason against the king, the informant shall not be made to pay; rather, the perpetrator himself shall dispute the matter.
The legal dispute, having been presented for deliberation, consists of eighteen points. There are other points here as well, which the king himself should investigate:
the seizure of a sixth part [of treasure], pure [theft], violation of agreements, and treasure-troves.
Killing, seizure, theft, and the violation of prohibitions or royal commands.
Neither the king nor his official should personally initiate a legal case;
he should reduce excessive claims and fulfill those that are deficient.
One should cause [the document] to be entered upon the ground for as long as the matter remains undecided;
it must be heard, written down, corrected, and deliberated upon.
Then the presiding judge shall cause the plaintiff's case, as stated by himself, to be written on a wooden board with chalk; thereafter, it shall be refined and recorded on the official document.
"But those who, after the matter has been stated and accepted, reach a settlement between themselves,
one should impose a fine upon them in accordance with the nature of the legal claim."
Or others who create opposition against cities, villages, great kings, or assemblies—
all such legal proceedings are proclaimed to be inadmissible.
One should first write on a wooden board or on the ground using chalk; having corrected what is deficient or excessive, one should subsequently enter it into the document.
When the plaintiff, due to lack of confidence, is unable to speak,
time should be granted to him in accordance with his capacity and the nature of the case.
If [the judge] is unable [to decide] where two parties desire to conduct a lawsuit,
then a period of time must be granted there to both the plaintiff and the defendant.
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is fourfold, and likewise the counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*);
the final determination (*nirṇaya*) is said to be fourfold, though some maintain it is eightfold.
Place, time, as well as location and configuration,
the name of the knower, residence, measurement, and the name of the field.
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should record these ten things: the father's name, the grandfather's name, and the mention of previous kings.
Or he may obtain a postponement for three days or even seven days,
until such time as the intellect of the one desiring to speak arises in the dispute.
Even a lawsuit involving many claims that has been settled in legal proceedings,
the king may, if he so desires, take it up again out of a desire to discover the truth.
Accusation based on suspicion, the truth, a request regarding a matter to be examined,
and a renewed legal proceeding when a case has been concluded— these are to be known as the four kinds of plaints.

Delusion is defined as doubt; it is necessarily the perception of a lost object. Delusion is also the solicitation for what has already been obtained, as well as the repeated performance of actions regarding what has already occurred.
He who has been dismissed by the king, he who causes opposition among the citizens,
or likewise he who opposes the entire kingdom as well as its constituent elements;
He who does not wish to act justly, or who acts unjustly,
and likewise he who does not cause it to be recorded in writing— his case shall not succeed.
Where both contradictory and non-contradictory meanings are found established in a single [textual passage], one should avoid that position from afar.
The Reply] [1.3.0] But when such a thesis has been formulated by the proponent,
then the opponent should provide a reply connected to that thesis.
When the prima facie case has been determined, distinguished as to what is acceptable and what is unacceptable,
and when it has been formally stated and stabilized, one should then cause the reply to be written down.
[1.3.1 Time should be granted to one who requests it: Where a defendant requests time due to timidity, fear, or likewise due to a lapse of memory, he deserves to obtain that time.
For one day, three days, five days, seven days, or even a fortnight;
for a month, three months, four months, or a year—he receives [the fruit] according to his capacity.

Those who know it declare that a reply is one that pervades the entire position (*pakṣa*), is essential, free from doubt, and unconfused; it is such that it does not require further explanation to be understood. (BP 1.3.005)

The reply is of four kinds: the direct reply (*sampratipatti*), the false reply (*mithyottara*), the reply based on prior judgment (*prāṅnyāyottara*), and the reply based on a special reason (*kāraṇottara*).
However, he who does not provide a reply that corresponds to the facts of the plaintiff's case...
One who has witnessed [the offense] should be made to pay [the fine], employing means such as conciliation and the rest.
Conciliation is speech preceded by pleasant words; sowing dissension is the display of fear; punishment consists of the deprivation of wealth, as well as beating and imprisonment.

Bṛhaspati states that in cases of violence, theft, verbal or physical assault, false accusations regarding cattle, and likewise in matters of urgency, one may dispute over land immediately, even outside the prescribed legal season.

One who speaks inconsistently, one who evades the legal procedure, one who fails to appear, one who offers no reply, and one who flees after being summoned— these five are declared to be defeated. In cases of defiling a maiden, theft, quarrel, and acts of violence, [the defendant is defeated] even if he does not plead.
In cases of bribery and false testimony, one should initiate a lawsuit immediately.
In the case of a milch cow, a draft ox, a field, women, and likewise in procreation; as well as in the matter of a deposit, a loan for use, a gift, and in buying and selling.

In a case of prior claim (*prāṅnyāya*) and when a reason (*kāraṇa*) is stated, the defendant (*pratyarthin*) shall point out the proof (*kriyā*); but in a case of denial (*mithyā*), the plaintiff (*pūrvavādī*) shall do so; however, this does not apply in a case of confession (*praipatti*).
Where a proponent advances a position without stating a reason, that should be known as an admission (*pratipatti*); the reason, however, is a separate thing, namely the rejoinder (*uttara*).
But he who, having engaged in all manner of conversation, should converse with another even in private,
must be made to pay the entire amount, according to Bṛhaspati when he is sued.
In cases of verbal assault and disputes over land, one should avoid divine ordeals;
likewise, when there is a connection to the sale or receipt of property, one should not employ the ordeal of sacred libation if the party is unwilling.
[1.3.2 The Fourfold Reply] If a defendant who has been formally charged should deny the charge,
one should recognize that as a false reply according to legal procedure.
If, upon hearing the charge, the defendant admits it,
that is declared by those learned in the scriptures to be "admission" (*sampratipatti*).
If the defendant, having been confronted with the claim by the plaintiff,
admits that very matter and states a reason for it, that is indeed a plea of counter-claim (*pratyavaskandana*).
If the defendant, having been confronted with the claim asserted by the plaintiff,
admits it to be so and states the grounds for it, Manu has declared that he is not to be held at fault.
If one who has been defeated by conduct is made to write [an admission] again, he is to be punished as previously defeated; that is called a *prāṅnyāya* (previous judgment).
One should employ the truth when it is true, and one should record falsehood when it is false;
likewise, one should state the reason when there is a reason, and victory when there has been victory.
A confession arising from fear or delusion is considered false and is censured by those who know the scriptures; however, a confession made in truth is declared to be righteous.
When a legal case is brought forward, the truth has been declared by the virtuous to be praiseworthy;
that which is contrary [to the truth] is unrighteous, and the defendant shall incur defeat.
When the plaintiff and the defendant both arrive at the same time out of a desire for precedence,
the trial must be conducted according to the order of their castes, while also taking into account the relative gravity of their suffering.
When the defendant has been brought at the same time as the plaintiff in the presence of the members of the court,
he shall then write his reply (uttara) corresponding to the words of the plaint.
The rule regarding the meaning of the suffixes has been explained in the presentation of connected meanings;
now, that which is to be grasped among the fourfold types [of suffixes] is being stated.

One should not characterize that which is other than the subject at hand, that which is neutral, that which is deficient or excessive, that which is irrelevant, that which lacks an expressible essence, that which is doubtful, or that which is contrary.
If he causes fear, or creates a division, or employs intimidation or obstruction,
he who does these things loses his case in legal proceedings.
But when an officiating priest or others have been appointed, both are declared to be equal;
in the sacrifice, the master obtains merit, while in the debate, he obtains either loss or victory.
Where the plaintiff or the defendant dies after the plaint and the reply have been written down, their son shall clear up the legal dispute on their behalf.
If a legal dispute remains undecided, the king would be deceived;
the granting of victory would not be impartial. Therefore, he should settle all cases.
But if one points out witnesses yet does not bring them to trial within thirty nights or three fortnights, his case suffers defeat.
One who flees after being summoned, one who remains silent, one defeated by the testimony of witnesses,
and one who admits the claim by his own statement— these are the four kinds of litigants who lose their case.
One who flees is defeated after three fortnights; one who remains silent, after seven days;
one whose testimony is contradicted by witnesses, at that very moment; and one who admits the claim, likewise.
Failing to state what has been presented, not appearing in court, maintaining silence regarding the meaning of one's own position, and these are the characteristics of one who is losing the case.
People know him to be possessed [of sin] who, in an assembly, endures being accused of a mortal transgression, a minor offense, or a grave crime.
Therefore, a wise person should strive with effort to purify the self;
whatever task is most important, that one should first purify.
He who is accused of a mortal sin and desires to escape from that transgression must first accept [the ordeal]; having been defeated by it, he deserves punishment.
When a divine ordeal has been performed for the purpose of establishing conduct, and after the defendant has been summoned and the time fixed,
if anyone does not present himself, one must not allow a pretext to be made in that case.
If, at that time, a fault caused by fate or the king should occur,
he shall not be defeated merely by the abandonment of his security deposit.
When a legal dispute has been initiated and is proceeding between a plaintiff and a defendant,
those who settle it between themselves shall be made to pay a fine double the amount in question.
When the claims of the plaintiff and the defendant have been set forth and the determination of the case has begun,
a settlement between the two heated parties may occur like that of two pieces of iron [being joined].
[1.3.3 Examination of the Sandhi] But if there is a disagreement between the witnesses and the assessors regarding both parties,
those who are discerning should effect a reconciliation between them while they remain wavering like a swing.
Where there is equality of strength but a difference in either scriptural tradition or conduct,
a peace treaty with that king is recommended for both parties.
Where the law and the judicial proceeding are subject to doubt regarding their respective portions,
a reconciliation should be made there, just as between two pieces of heated iron.

Then a peace treaty on equal terms should be made, for an unequal one will cease to hold; through equality, the king gains the support of righteousness and wealth, as well as fame. Witnesses and members of the court do not suffer, and enmity comes to an end.
Punishment, restraint, and favor, as well as dharma, fame, and infamy—
these arise for men from conflict, and likewise, further fault arises from it.

Therefore, what those presiding over the family and the guild— who know the law, who are impartial in view, and who are free from hatred and greed— may declare, that should be done by one who understands.
Section on Legal Action] [1.4.0] When the written statement has been properly scrutinized and found to be faultless,
the burden of proof (kriyā) is required from either the defendant or the plaintiff.
But for those who remain in the court, the members of the assembly shall conduct the investigation;
after the respondent has properly stated his answer, it must be given to one of the litigants.

[1.4.1 The Strength and Weakness of the Means of Proof] The proponent shall establish his claim; likewise, the opponent shall establish the grounds for his defense. The proponent shall establish victory through a certificate of victory based on the account of what transpired previously.
What was written in the first quarter [of the plaint] exactly as it stands, in its entirety,
the plaintiff shall establish by means of action in the third quarter.
Having heard both the former and the latter [statements], once the burden of proof has been assigned by the members of the court,
he who asserts it must substantiate his entire claim by means of written documents and other evidence.
Action is said to be of two kinds: human and likewise divine. Each of these is divided into many types by the seers who know the truth.
Human action is recorded in tradition as being threefold: witnesses, written documents, and possession.
The divine proof (*daivī kriyā*) is ninefold, beginning with the balance (*dhaṭa*) and ending with that born of *dharma*;
the human proof (*mānuṣī kriyā*) is threefold: witnesses, documents, and inference.
Witnesses are recorded as being of twelve kinds, while documents are traditionally held to be of eight types.
Inference is said to be threefold, while divine procedure is ninefold. In the first or the third [stage], both divine and human means of proof are authoritative;
but in the subsequent fourth stage, there shall be witnesses along with the document of victory.
In matters such as debts and the like, one should employ human means of proof;
in a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) or a counter-plea (*pratyavaskanda*), the defendant himself must establish his case.

For the sake of the subsequent [point] and for the sake of the claim, the plaintiff may state a false answer; however, when witnesses are available, no divine ordeal is prescribed. Furthermore, when there is a written document in legal disputes, there shall be neither divine ordeal nor witnesses.
In cases of verbal assault, disputes over land, and indeed in all four types of violent crimes, divine means of proof must be diligently avoided.
In cases of treason against the king and in acts of violence, one should employ divine proof (*daivikī kriyā*).
One who steals gems, pearls, or corals by means of deception, a thief of nooses, a perpetrator of injury, or one who consorts with another's wife must always be examined by means of oaths.
In cases of accusations involving mortal sins, in the misappropriation of a deposit, and likewise in cases of theft,
the king should examine the matter by means of ordeals even when witnesses are present.
If doubt arises regarding a written document or the testimony of witnesses, [he should proceed with an ordeal].
And when inference is confused, divine proof is the means of purification in that case.
When a dispute concerning gambling or betting has arisen,
witnesses are declared to be the means of proof, not ordeals nor written documents. The king should cause a decision to be made by those witnesses as they may be available.
In cases of violence, verbal disputes, physical assault,
and matters arising from force, witnesses and even divine ordeals are admissible.
In the case of a debt, documentary evidence, witnesses, or even a trace of circumstantial reasoning may be employed.
Or, out of a desire for the welfare of the subjects,

a divine ordeal may be prescribed; when witnesses are long-standing yet have become silent, or when they have perished, or when inferential evidence is corrupted, one should settle the case by means of ordeals.
[1.5. Witnesses] There should be nine, seven, five, four, or even three witnesses; or two who are both learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and renowned. One should never question only one person.
The keeper of the gambling hall, the receiver of the stakes, and likewise one who is present within the proceedings—
each of these, as well as the king and his superintendent, may serve as a witness.
Thieves, violent assailants, eunuchs, gamblers, and informers—these are not witnesses because of their wickedness; witness-status does not exist among them. [1.5.1 Witnesses]
The written, the secret, the reminded, the one by family, the messenger, the incidental,
the subsequent, and another which occurs in the midst of a legal matter.
The king, the official, and likewise the village headman—these are recorded as the twelve kinds of witnesses.
I shall explain their distinctions correctly and in due order.

He by whom [the document] is written, including his own caste, name, and so forth, as well as that of his father and his place of residence— he is to be known as a witness designated as "written" (likhitasaṃjñaka).
When a debtor has performed an act such as the repayment of a debt through various means,
and that act is recorded in the presence [of witnesses], it is called a *lekhitaka* (a written document).
But he who is made to hear the statement regarding a debt while separated by a wall,
and who denies it as it truly is, is called a concealed witness.
One who is summoned and made a witness in matters such as debts, deposits, or transactions,
and who is repeatedly reminded, is declared to be a "reminded witness" (*smārita*).
In matters of partitioning or sale, a kinsman who is useful to both parties— one who knows the law and belongs to the same lineage— is proclaimed as a *kulya*.
He who, being sent by the plaintiff and the defendant, listens to their statements and is approved by both as a virtuous person, is declared to be a *dūtaka* (messenger/witness).
But when a matter is being transacted, whoever comes of his own accord and says, "You have been named as our witness here," he is an incidental witness.

Where a witness departs for another region or is about to die, he should cause someone else to hear the testimony in due order; one should know that person to be the subsequent witness (*uttarasākṣin*).
Among witnesses also, he who, while they are testifying one after another, hears it repeatedly from each hearing, is a witness designated as "subsequent" (uttara).
He whose confidence is placed in both [parties] and who is informed of their business,
as well as one who enters into the midst of the proceedings while remaining hidden, should be known as a *gūḍhadhārī* (a secret agent).
Whatever statement of the plaintiff and the defendant has been heard by the king himself,
he alone shall be the witness in that case, even in the event of a disagreement between the two.
But when a legal case has been decided and a retrial occurs, the presiding officer together with the members of the court shall act as witnesses therein; it cannot be otherwise.
Where a dwelling has been occupied and covered on all sides up to the boundary, that village shall be considered a witness even if it has been cut off; of this there is no doubt.
Two who have been written down, as well as two who are secret, three, four, or five who have been recorded;
those who appear spontaneously, those reminded of the case, kinsmen, and likewise superior witnesses.
A messenger who holds his own seal, one present at the time of the transaction,
and likewise the king or an official witness— each of these alone may be authoritative.

[1.5.2 Description of the Faults of Witnesses and Punishment for the Corrupt] If a litigant should impugn a witness designated by the party with a fault when he is not actually at fault, he deserves a fine equal to the value of the claim. If he impugns one who is truly at fault, he shall be punished accordingly.
Whatever defects of the document may exist, as well as those attributed to the witnesses, must be stated at the time of the trial; one should not raise them after they have already been stated.
The defects of the witnesses must be set forth by the defendant in court;
having written all of them down on the document, the reply must then be stated.
Those who have acted as witnesses in a previous proceeding are never eligible to serve as witnesses again;
therefore, they must be treated otherwise by the defendant in the current legal action.

If the defendant clearly fails to prove his case through witnesses, he shall be compelled to pay a fine; likewise, all witnesses who have been proven false are to be deprived of their witness-status according to the law of witnesses.
Whether it be the defendant or the plaintiff, when proving a defect in the witness by means relevant to the matter at hand,
there shall be no separate legal proceeding.

If the plaintiff has no further desire for more and the witness remains established in the truth, then that defeated party shall be made to pay a fine according to the disciplinary procedure prescribed by the scriptures.
But he who, when the matter has been stated, impeaches witnesses who were previously unimpeachable and does not state the grounds for that [impeachment], shall incur the first amercement.
In a legal dispute, if the documents or the witnesses of either party are found to be tainted, that party's case shall not be adjudicated until those [tainted elements] have been cleared.
When a decision has been reached through the testimony of witnesses and the members of the court, if anyone initiates a renewed dispute, the king shall investigate that matter.
When witnesses are suspected of corruption, the purification of the witnesses must first be carried out;
once the witnesses have been cleared, one should thereafter purify the legal matter itself.
The members of the assembly, who are conversant with the meaning of the treatises on Dharma, should address [the witness] with words praising truth and rejecting falsehood:
"Whatever merit has been earned by you from birth until death— "
All that goes to ruin through the false accusation of one who is innocent.
A false witness, a false judge, and a slayer of a Brahmin are declared to be equal;
among these, a killer of an embryo or a betrayer of a friend is said to be no greater [in sin].
Having understood this, the witness who speaks the truth thereby attains fame in this world and a fortunate rebirth in the next.
There are men who, out of greed, might state a matter falsely;
and there are others, evil-minded men, who forge false documents.
I shall now describe those witnesses who are to be questioned, as well as those lowest of men who are to be excluded, as prescribed by the scriptures.
Those engaged in the performance of Śrauta and Smārta rites, free from greed and hatred,
of noble birth, irreproachable, and endowed with austerity, charity, and compassion, are qualified witnesses.
[1.5.3 Non-witnesses] The father of the mother, the paternal uncle, the brother-in-law, the maternal uncle,
the brother, the friend, and the son-in-law are non-witnesses in legal disputes concerning debts.
Those addicted to other men's wives or to drinking, gamblers, those previously discredited,
the insane, the afflicted, the violent, and atheists are not to be witnesses.

Even virtuous persons do not constitute valid witnesses [if they testify] after the death of the owner of the property; however, those who were informed by the owner himself when he was near death may serve as witnesses for his son.
Having removed his sandals and turban, he should raise his right hand;
taking gold, cow dung, and darbha grass, he should speak the truth.
Those who have presented themselves should be examined by means of their voice, complexion, gestures, and so forth.

Even if one must speak falsehoods, one should protect a Brahmin who has committed an offense through a single lapse of heedlessness, one who is afflicted by a calamity, or one being beaten by soldiers and the like.
If the entire subject matter of the plaint is corroborated by the witnesses, he shall be the victor; otherwise, however, he shall not obtain the object of his proof.
If a witness who is free from illness does not come when summoned,
he shall be made to pay the debt and a fine after three fortnights have passed.

[1.5.4 Examination of the Strength and Weakness of Witnesses] In a conflict between witnesses, those who are more numerous should be accepted; if they are equal in number, those endowed with good qualities;
if there is a conflict between those of good qualities, those engaged in virtuous action; and if they are equal in that regard, those who are most pure.
Witnesses who, when not questioned, speak the truth, as well as those who do not answer a question when asked, shall be restrained, censured, and punished according to the law.
If that which has been recited is complete with respect to place, time, age, substance, name, caste, and measure,
one should point out the object to be accomplished as established.
In cases where there may be disagreement regarding place, time, age, substance, quantity, appearance, or species,
the testimony must likewise not be otherwise [than truthful].

When the categories of the matter have been specified and the witness has been summoned to testify, if he does not speak, his testimony is as good as that of a game of dice; it shall not be considered formally declared.
In the first half [of the debate], one should present the entire thesis as it was stated;
however, that which was spoken with deficiency or excess shall not be considered as having been formally declared.
Where witnesses state a matter either less than or more than what it actually is, that matter should be understood as not having been stated; this is declared to be the rule regarding witnesses.
When the portion of the matter to be proven has been recounted by the witnesses, the entire case shall be considered established.
In cases of sexual intercourse with women, acts of violence, and theft, that which is to be proven is determined [by the evidence].
But where testimony is deficient or excessive, one should reject it; in such a case, the witness shall not be punished, for he deserves punishment for failing to speak.
[1.6. Written Evidence] [1.6.0] This determination regarding the number and characteristics of witnesses has been declared;
now I shall state the rules for written evidence in their proper order.
Since confusion may arise even regarding matters such as debts at the time of agreement,
the Creator created letters and placed them upon paper in ancient times.
[1.6.1 Characteristics of a Written Document] A document is said to be that which is consistent with local custom, which records the increase in years, months, fortnights,
and so forth, and which bears the hand-signatures of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe.
[1.6.2 Varieties of Documents] A royal edict, one executed by a local official, and likewise one written in one's own hand—
document is said to be of these three kinds; furthermore, it is divided in many ways.
Documentary evidence in common practice is sevenfold, consisting of [deeds concerning] shares, gifts, purchase, pledges, agreements, slaves, and debts; royal edicts are of three kinds.
The document known as the *vibhāga-patra* is prescribed for the determination of shares; when a boundary dispute has been settled, the document is traditionally called the *sīmā-patra*.
A deed of gift, a deed of partition, and likewise a deed concerning boundaries; a deed of purchase, a deed of slavery, and after that, a deed of mortgage.
A written agreement, a document of victory,
and likewise a treaty— these are of many kinds according to the differences in their legal transactions.
A document for a pledge should be for the purpose of a loan, and a document for a slave should be for the purpose of a slave.
For the sake of accomplishing their desired objectives, villages, guilds, corporations,
and other such groups may establish a charter of agreement for the purpose of dharma, provided it does not contradict the sacred scriptures.
When brothers who have already divided their inheritance execute a document among themselves by mutual consent, that is called a *bhāgalekhya* (a deed of partition).
But when one, having given land, should execute a document valid for as long as the moon and sun endure—
a document of gift that is neither to be cut off nor to be taken away— that they know to be a *dānalekhya*.
Having purchased a house, field, or similar property, that document which one causes to be executed, containing the equal price and the names [of the parties],
is called a *kraya-lekhya* (deed of purchase).
That document which one executes after giving movable or immovable property as a pledge,
and which involves the acts of custody or enjoyment, is known as a *ādhi-lekhya* (mortgage deed).
When a village or a district should mutually execute a document concerning liquor,
provided it does not conflict with the king and pertains to matters of dharma or wealth, they call that a *saṃvitpatra* (contractual deed).
"If one who is destitute of clothing and food in the wilderness writes,
'I shall perform whatever work you command,' that is recognized as a document of slavery."
Having received money at interest, one may either perform the work oneself or cause it to be done by another;
this is declared by the wise to be an *uddhāra-patra*, a document for a debt.
Regarding the established custom of guilds, corporations, assemblies, and the like, the proof thereof is documentary evidence; neither divine ordeals nor witnesses are required.
But for the purpose of maintaining the agreement of guilds, corporations,
and the like, that which is established is called a *sthitipatra* by those who know the *smṛtis* of Manu and others.

[1.6.3 The King’s Edict on Giving] Having bestowed land and other gifts, the king should cause a charter to be prepared— whether on a copper plate or a cloth— recording the Dharma and including the location, lineage, and other relevant details.
"For the merit of my mother, father, and myself,
this gift is given by me today to such-and-such a fellow-student, the son of such-and-such."
It is unseizable and irremovable, free from all future liabilities,
coeval with the moon and the sun, and descending through the lineage of sons and grandsons.

He who severs a gift shall write down the fruit of that act as follows: heaven for the giver and protector, and indeed hell for the taker; for sixty thousand years is the result of cutting off a gift.

The year, month, and so forth, along with the oceanic signs, accompanied by the signature of the Superintendent of Revenue, and written by the scribes of peace and war, stating: "This has been known by me."
Such a royal edict is declared to be "written by favor" (*prasādalikhita*),
which the king issues to someone, recording his country and other particulars.
But that which is written by one who is pleased with service, valor, and so forth, is indeed a document of favor (*prasāda*).

[1.6.5 Judgment Document] When, at the conclusion of the determination following the arguments and counter-arguments of the plaintiff and defendant, the king grants a written document to the victor, that is called a judgment document (*jayapatra*).
Whatever has occurred in the legal proceeding, beginning with the plaint and the reply,
along with the evidence and the determination [of the case], he shall write all of this in the document of victory (*jayapatra*).
He shall establish the matter to be proved (*sādhya*) in accordance with the victory, which consists of four parts.
And a document of victory is required to be provided with the royal seal.
To those other than those who have failed in their arguments and so forth, [the judgment] is granted;
and that, being established by a recital of the proceedings, shall be the document of victory (*jayapatra*).
[1.6.6 Defects of Documents] A document executed by one who is about to die, by one whose means are diminished or lost, by one who is insane,
afflicted by calamity, or produced under the influence of poison or fraud, is not valid.
Where a single witness who is tainted or censured is appointed, that document is a forged one;
so too is it when the scribe is of such a character.

A document that is bright [in appearance], yet written long ago; or one that is soiled, though of recent date; or one that is broken and contains corrupt syllables—such a document shall be considered forged.
Just as a reflection situated in a mirror appears to exist though it is non-existent,
so too do skillful people create paintings that possess the likeness of forms.
For a proof is established by truth, while a refutation is indeed by means of a fault;
thus, that which is found to be defective in the royal court is indeed subjected to investigation.
Having deliberated together with the Brahmins, he should examine the faults of the speaker.
By that [same criterion] by which witnesses, scribes, and executors fall into falsehood, by that the document shall be deemed corrupt; one should declare it pure when those [parties] are pure.
If a debtor denies a debt that has been entered in writing with his own hand,
he may be compelled to pay by means of witnesses recorded in the document, by oral testimony, or with the consent of the scribe.

"But when letters are displaced from their positions, lack clarity, are ambiguous, or have deviated from their proper characteristics— if they stand thus, Bhṛgu declares that the document is defective."
The plaintiff shall produce the document; however, if he has died while being sued, his son shall produce the possession alone.
If he too has died, his son shall produce that [possession].
Having ascertained the matter, forgers who are skilled in place and time produce a document resembling it; one should examine that with great care.
Some skilled people write a document as if it were a painting;
therefore, it is held that the establishment [of a fact] based solely on the power of a document is not absolute.

Relatives deceive women, children, the afflicted, and those ignorant of writing by having them sign a document marked with their own names; such a document must be scrutinized through logical reasoning and the examination of circumstances.
When an error arises in this threefold document,
one should then correct it by the written statement of the hand of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe.

An "exertion" (*udyāma*) is known to exist where a fraudulent condition (*upadhi*) has been made, characterized by the undertaking [of a task] for the sake of receiving a profit, the acquisition of the fruit, and the possession of wealth from the counter-party. (BP 1.6.044)
Whatever has been shown at the proper time, whatever has been heard, and whatever has been reminded—
such a document is established as valid in all cases, even when the witnesses have died.
Where the capacity of the syllables as signifiers is impaired,
there would be the total destruction of actions and an infinite regress would arise.
A document that is more than thirty years old, and which has neither been seen nor heard of,
does not attain validity, even though witnesses may still be living.
But when the profit has been realized, if the debtor does not produce the written document nor demand it from the creditor, he shall incur doubt regarding the matter.

For guilds, trade associations, corporations, and the like, it has been shown that [the king] should cause [their rules] to be heard and remembered at the appropriate time; in this way, they shall become more authoritative.
If something has been obtained, or if there is a formal designation [of ownership] in that manner,
the document itself is the authority even if the witnesses have died.
When a wealthy person standing nearby has not been requested for a loan by one who is capable [of asking],
that document will be rendered weak due to the suspicion that it is a pure debt [without a prior agreement].
A document executed by those who are insane, idiotic, or weak; by those traveling out of fear of the king; or by those who are timid, fearful, or afflicted, shall not be subject to loss.
Now, if a scribe together with the witnesses has met his death,
that [document] is undoubtedly purified by their own handwriting and other such evidence.
When there is doubt regarding a debt, whether the debtor is living or dead,
that debt is settled by other documents written in his own hand.

When doubt arises regarding a document, [it should be resolved] by the witnesses, the scribe, and the maker; if they are found to be corrupt, [the authenticity is determined] by means of previous characters written by their own hands and other such evidence.
A written document is never superseded by witnesses or by an oath.
One incurs loss through neglect by means of non-appearance and non-announcement.
Therefore, both of these must be examined by the king with particular care;
indeed, there should be only one written document for the accomplishment of a single matter.
But among many documents, one may find defects:
that which is contrary to local custom, that which is ambiguous, that which lacks proper sequence,
that which was executed by one who is not the owner, and that which is deficient in its subject matter— such a document is defective.
[1.7. Enjoyment] [1.7.0] All activities have wealth as their root, and all efforts are considered to be for its attainment;
its prescribed method consists of increase, protection, and enjoyment.
Furthermore, that [wealth] is to be known as threefold: pure, variegated, and black;
therein, the classification is further to be understood as sevenfold.

Wealth acquired through learning, heroism, austerity, a daughter, a pupil, a sacrificial client, or inheritance— this sevenfold wealth is [the basis for] the fee (śulka), for both [the teacher and the giver] are of that same nature in respect to it.
That which is acquired through usury, agriculture, trade, customs duties, the practice of crafts,
or from one who has received a favor, is declared to be "spotted" (śabala).
That which is acquired through gambling with dice and the like, by means of messengers, by fraudulent objects, through violence, or by deceit, is declared to be "black" wealth.
By means of that [title], purchase, sale, giving, and receiving,
as well as various other transactions and the enjoyment of property, are carried out.
Whatever a man performs with a particular kind of material substance,
he obtains a corresponding fruit for that, both after death and in this world.
Furthermore, that [dharma] is traditionally held to be twelvefold, based on the respective castes;
it is threefold as common to all, while the remainder is traditionally held to be ninefold.
That which has descended by order of succession, that which is given out of affection, and that which is acquired together with the wife—
these three kinds of property are declared to belong to all castes without distinction.
The specific wealth of a Brāhmaṇa should be known as having three characteristics:
that which is obtained through acceptance of gifts, that which is received from a patron for officiating at sacrifices, and likewise that which is received from a pupil.
They say that the specific wealth of a Kṣatriya is also of three kinds: that acquired in battle, from taxes, and from fines in legal proceedings.
The specific wealth of a Vaiśya is also to be known as having three characteristics:
agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade; while for a Śūdra, it consists of service to these [other classes].
For all social classes alike, this is the lawful way of acquiring wealth;
by the opposite method it becomes unlawful, unless there is a grave emergency.

In times of distress, the practice of the next lower order is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa; however, the occupation of a Vaiśya is also declared for him, but never that of a Śūdra under any circumstances.
A Brāhmaṇa should by no means perform the work of a Śūdra, nor should a Śūdra perform the work of a Brāhmaṇa; for those two acts lead to their respective fall.
Neither superior nor inferior action exists for those two;
for, setting aside intermediate actions, they are common to all.

Having crossed over a time of distress while supporting his dependents by the occupation of a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa should relinquish that Kṣatriya occupation once he has performed purification for himself.
But that Brāhmaṇa who takes delight in that very occupation out of passion—
a fallen man from the path— is proclaimed as a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*, marked by his transgression.
"He who, having cast his own family behind him, indeed goes to the family of another—
by that evil conduct, he is known as a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*."
When the performance of legal business has been conducted during the day in villages and cities,
and when witnesses are available, no ordeal is to be employed as a means of proof.
In the case of doors, paths, construction, enjoyment, water-conduits, and the like, possession alone is weightier;
neither a written document nor witnesses are required.
This rule has been declared regarding witnesses and written documents;
now the procedure for the acquisition of immovable property and for possession is being stated.
