Through learning, by purchase, by marriage-portion, by inheritance from a heroic ancestor,
or by ancestral succession, immovable property belonging to a sapinda who is childless is obtained as a share in eight ways.
[1.7.2 Possession is of seven kinds] When possession is acquired through inheritance, purchase, gift, seizure, partition, valor,
or discovery— provided it has been obtained through these seven means— it attains validity as possession accompanied by legal title (*sāgama*).
That possession which has come down by succession, that which is based on a royal edict, or that which is accompanied by purchase or a formal grant—
such possession alone attains legal validity.
Immovable property acquired through partition, purchase, inheritance from a father, or received from a king attains legal validity by being enjoyed; it is lost through neglect.
When someone has taken possession and enjoyed what was obtained—having accepted it without opposition—he acquires ownership of it; however, through neglect, he suffers loss.
If one's possession has been uninterrupted for thirty years, beginning from the time of occupation, and it has not been contested, one shall not displace that person from it.

There shall be no enjoyment of property belonging to women, nor of the wealth of the king or of Śrotriyas, nor of the property of the mentally disabled or minors, without a written document in any case whatsoever.
One shall not obtain success through possession alone; nor even through a pure title deed. Success is achieved through both, and not otherwise.
In the case of the property of a child or a Vedic scholar, and when it has been obtained from the father in due order,
neither the one who took it nor his son should use force to recover it during its enjoyment.
The law regarding cattle, women, men, and so forth is established [as follows]:
if a village, a field, or a garden is recorded in a single legal document.
Even when only a portion has been enjoyed, all [the parts] are considered enjoyed;
for where even a small amount of enjoyment exists, title alone possesses no force.
An eyewitness is superior to inference; a written document is more authoritative than eyewitnesses;
and possession by three successive generations, when unopposed, is weightier than these.
Inference [is established] when a witness resides there until death; however, a document and possession that are uncontradicted are authoritative for three generations.
If one's father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are all living,
yet land has been enjoyed for thirty years without being obstructed by others;

That possession is to be known as "personal" (*pauruṣī*); it is double for two persons (*dvipuruṣī*), and triple for three persons (*tripūruṣī*); beyond that, it becomes "long-standing" (*cirantanā*).
Where the one who brings forward the claim is challenged, then the document and the witness are the primary authorities;
but in their absence, possession alone is the most weighty proof among the sons.
The original acquirer shall establish possession or title in the assembly;
his son shall establish only possession; but his grandson and those following him need establish nothing at all.
If property is given openly by others to one who is not the heir,
yet another person subsequently enjoys it, that first person is not entitled to recover it.
If one, while witnessing another giving away land, does not restrain him,
he shall not regain that land even by means of a valid document.
Bhṛgu says that whether given by the heirs themselves or by others, that [gift] belongs to him alone;
possession for three generations is established for others, there is no doubt in this matter.
However, as long as the sapinda relationship has not ceased, it is not established for the sakulyas.
However, that which has been enjoyed by one who is not the owner— such as a house, field, or shop—
does not lapse [to the ownership of another] through such enjoyment by a friend, relative, or kinsman.
For one learned in the Vedas, merit is inexhaustible; for one who grants safety to the king's men, there is affection among kinsmen; and food eaten by these [three] is never lost.
Food consumed at a wedding by those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), as well as by the king and his ministers,
does not become pure for them even after a very long period of time.
In the case of those who are incapable, lazy, afflicted by disease, children, fearful, or away on travel,
a document executed by another does not lose its validity through such possession.
When a doubt arises regarding a house or field whose enjoyment has been interrupted,
one should establish its purity through a written document, or by means of witnesses who are familiar with the possession.

Those who know the names of the parties, the arrival at the boundary markers, the number, the time, the direction and location, and the cause for the enjoyment or the interruption of possession, are witnesses in that matter.

Those who have been born [in the vicinity], those who reside very near, and those who dwell in other regions—these are designated as the primary witnesses; they should be questioned for the determination of the legal matter.
Whatever those who are uncorrupted and impartial may say regarding a doubtful matter, that must be accepted as authoritative; in this way, dharma is not lost.
This has been declared concerning immovable property as the means of establishing ownership and enjoyment.
But in a case where the statement lacks supporting evidence, the divine ordeal (divyā kriyā) must be prescribed.
Even if it has been enjoyed by three other kings without formal title,
a grant to Brahmins must never be seized by a king.
Where possession has been exercised by three generations and continues into the fourth, that enjoyment attains stability; one need not inquire about the title anywhere.
When property has been enjoyed by three generations of persons without being prohibited, no legal title need be produced there; in that case, possession is more weighty.
In disputes concerning immovable property, possession extending over three generations is to be known as independent; it is indeed the authoritative means for determining the matter to be proved.
If possession has been held for three generations and is accompanied by a valid written document,
such a gift to a Brahmin (*brahmadeya*) cannot be taken away from him.
If possession has been held by three generations in succession,
it cannot be overturned except by a prior royal edict.
If land has been enjoyed for three generations by someone while it was openly available and unopposed,
that land must not be taken away from him, unless he should state a title based on a legal right.
In the legal treatise, possession is powerful when it is uninterrupted and long-standing;
indeed, even that which was interrupted is to be known as such if it was previously established.
If property has been enjoyed by the father according to custom and in accordance with dharma,
even after he has died, that property is acquired by him through such enjoyment.
But when land has been enjoyed by three persons in due order according to the law,
in the absence of documentary evidence, a fourth person may acquire it there.

When property has been enjoyed by kinsmen of the same lineage, by relatives, or likewise by one's own kin, there can be no legal proof of ownership based on that enjoyment alone; in such cases, one must establish possession through other means.
Possession with title, long duration, uninterrupted and undisputed,
the presence of the opponent, and actual enjoyment— possession is thus fivefold.
Quadrupeds, wealth, grain, and so forth, suffer loss after one year; likewise, non-enjoyment of land, failure to produce a document at the proper time,
and the failure to recall witnesses are causes for the loss of one's own right.
Therefore, one must diligently maintain the authority of the means of proof;
by that, both immovable and movable matters are successfully accomplished.
In a case where there are no witnesses or where the matter was committed long ago, one should question the subsequent witnesses,
or subject the defendant to oaths, or employ a test by ordeal.
And there is the non-obstruction of teaching, as well as a brief summary of the reasoning.
Property stolen by thieves must be recovered from all [suspects] and restored;
if it cannot be found, it must be paid from the king's own treasury, otherwise he would incur the guilt of a thief.
[1.8. Divine Means] [1.8.0] Thus has been declared the means for establishing gain and enjoyment regarding immovable property;
however, in a legal proceeding lacking other evidence, divine proof is faultless.
When inferential means of proof have failed, one should clear the matter by means of divine ordeals.
The divine ordeals are recorded as being of nine kinds, beginning with the balance and ending with the *dharmaja* (the ordeal of truth).
The balance, fire, water, poison, and fifthly, the *kośa* (the ordeal of the sacred libation);
The sixth is said to be rice-grains, and the seventh is that *māṣaka*.
The eighth is said to be the time, and likewise the ninth is the dharma;
all these have been pointed out by the Self-Existent One through divine [vision].
[1.8.1 The Divine Arrangement] Since these [teachings] were employed by the great-souled gods for the sake of what is difficult to accomplish,
I shall state them as an outline for the purification of doubtful meanings.
These are applied in their proper sequence according to place, time, purpose, and number.
According to the sequence of offenses and with the intention of distinguishing between the virtuous and the non-virtuous,
these [penalties] should be administered according to the rule declared in the treatise, and not otherwise.
In matters such as debts, when there is mutual disagreement,
[the witnesses] should be made to pay [fines] corresponding to the value of the property, taking likewise into account the status of the persons involved.
For the purpose of worldly transactions, this designation has been declared on earth:
a coin struck from a karṣa of copper is to be known as a *kārṣika-paṇa*.
Four *suvarṇas* make one *niṣka*; a copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is a *paṇa*. A copper coin struck with a seal weighing one *karṣa* should be known as a *kārṣika-paṇa*.
That same [unit] is called a *cāndrikā*; four of those are *dhānakās*.
Twelve of those are a *suvarṇa*, which is also known as a *dīnāra*.
A fine of one thousand kārṣāpaṇas is the highest amercement;
half of that is declared the middle amercement, and half of that again is recorded as the lowest amercement.
A balance should be administered to a Brāhmaṇa, fire to a Kṣatriya,
water should be given to a Vaiśya, and poison indeed to a Śūdra.
The treasury is declared by the wise to be common to all [the members of the assembly].
Witnesses may fall into discord due to affection, anger, or greed;
however, no such discord ever arises regarding a divine ordeal administered according to the prescribed rule.
The ordeal should be administered according to the prescribed rules by those expert in ordeals; if it is administered contrary to the rules, then neither the proof nor the disproof is established.
Documents executed at an improper place or time, and those executed outside the presence of witnesses, always lead to failure in legal matters; of this there is no doubt.
Those expert in the administration of ordeals should administer the ordeal to one who is accused;
or, by mutual consent, either party may undergo it, while the other shall bear the head [of the animal used in the ordeal].

Even without a formal charge, one may administer an ordeal in cases of treason against the king or in the case of a mortal sin; this is declared to be the rule for the administration of ordeals, except by the king's command.
No one, however, should thus compel the accuser to undergo an ordeal.
[1.8.2 Divine Deities] Dharodhra, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa— these are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
BP1.8.020a. Between Deveśa and Īśāna is the path of the Ādityas.
BP1.8.020b. They are Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, and Bhaga.
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is remembered as the tenth;
after him Tvaṣṭṛ, then Viṣṇu, who is not the youngest, though born last.
Thus these twelve Ādityas have been proclaimed by their names.
To the western part of Agni, they know to be the abode of the Rudras:
Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, Girīśa, and the highly illustrious Mahāyaśas.
Ajaikapād,
Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and the unconquered Apratijita;
The lords of the worlds, Kapālī the lord of the people,
Sthāṇu, and the blessed Bhaga— these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.
One should designate the station of the Mothers between the Lord of the Dead and the Rakshasa;
namely, Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā accompanied by her hosts [are located there];
they know that the abode of Gaṇeśa is in the northern part of Nirṛti.
To the north of Varuṇa’s region, the abode of the Maruts is said to be located. [The names of the wind-gods are: Śvasana, Sparśana, Vāyu, Anila, and likewise Māruta.

[1.8.3 Divine Ordeals by Number] Manu has declared that the number [of coins] for divine ordeals begins with a *raśmi* and ends with a *kārṣāpaṇa*; one should employ it accordingly in the administration of justice.
When a thousand [paṇas] have been stolen, or when less than a quarter is missing, poison is used;
when less than three-quarters is missing, water; and when exactly half is missing, the balance (dhaṭa) should always be administered.
In a lawsuit involving four hundred [paṇas], a heated māṣaka coin must be administered;
for three hundred, rice grains are to be given, and for half of that amount, the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa) is prescribed.
When a hundred [kārṣāpaṇas] have been lost or stolen, the purification by ordeal must be administered.
The members of the court should diligently provide a ploughshare for one accused of stealing cattle;
or, in the case of the loss of half a yava, rice grains corresponding to that value.
Then, upon the destruction of half, a quarter, and an eighth [of the debt], both the [legal] and worldly procedures are considered applicable.
[1.8.4 The Procedure for Oaths] The mounts and weapons of the virtuous, as well as cattle, seeds, and gold;
the feet of gods and Brahmins, and the heads of one's sons and wife.
These oaths have been declared as always easy to perform in matters of small value; however, for violent crimes and grave accusations, they say that divine ordeals are the means of purification.
One should say "Speak! to a Brāhmaṇa; "Speak the truth! to a king;
[one should address] a Vaiśya with [the threat of] cows, seeds, and gold; and a Śūdra with all [possible] sins.
He should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by the truth, a Kṣatriya by his vehicles and weapons;
cowherds, merchants, artisans, and actors; as well as servants and usurers—he should treat these Brāhmaṇas no differently than Śūdras.
Those who have fallen away from their own duties, subsisting on the food of others,
yet desire the status of the twice-born— toward them one should behave as toward Śūdras.
Each person should be made to swear separately by means of oaths appropriate to their respective castes.
In matters concerning women, in marriages, regarding cattle, fuel, and food,
and in the case of a Brahmin’s misfortune, there is no sin in taking an oath.
Witnesses must give their testimony while standing within the court, and not elsewhere;
for this rule applies to all types of testimony, except in cases concerning immovable property.

If there is a dispute regarding the killing of living beings, one should state the testimony in the presence of the corpse; in its absence, however, one should state it in the presence of a identifying mark, and not otherwise.
Witnesses who have arrived at the place of dispute must not, unless they are questioned or appointed, intentionally speak the truth [only] when prompted; rather, they must testify with diligence.

The testimony of those witnesses, which is stated spontaneously and free from defects, is to be accepted; once they have spoken, however, the witnesses should not be questioned again and again by the king.
For those who have lived together with witnesses present, there is no rule for remarriage at all.
Likewise, the Seven Sages, Indra, and the others, whose wealth is their asceticism,
remained composed and uttered an oath at Puṣkara for the sake of mutual purification.
Within seven days, or within fourteen days, no misfortune caused by the king or by fate shall occur;
one becomes pure through oaths regarding wealth among kinsmen and sapindas.
When there is no human evidence whatsoever, a decision must be reached by means of divine proof alone;
however, when witnesses are available, a wise man should avoid recourse to divine methods.
In this manner, the number for those of low status is prescribed; for those of middle status, it is twice that amount;
and for those of superior status, it should be calculated as four times that by the examiners.
[1.8.5 The Procedure for the Balance] If the accused, when weighed on the balance, is lighter, he shall suffer loss;
but if he is equal, and then weighed again and is heavier, he shall be the victor.
In the event of the breaking of the scale-pan or the snapping of the axle, the king shall provide a new scale-pan;
the witnesses should be eminent Brāhmaṇas who speak according to what they have actually seen.
The king should appoint kinsmen who are pure yet free from greed;
the determination of purity or impurity is to be understood from their testimony.
In the case of the cutting of the side-posts, the breaking of the beam, or likewise of the *dhaṭa* and *karkaṭa*,
as well as the snapping of the rope or the failure of the axle, one shall incur impurity in the same manner.
[1.8.6 The Ritual of Fire] I shall proclaim the ritual of fire exactly as it is enjoined by the rules;
one should cause eight mandalas to be made in front, and likewise a ninth.
The first mandala is that of Agni; the second is remembered as belonging to Varuṇa;
the third has Vāyu as its deity; and the fourth has Yama as its deity.
The fifth, however, has Indra as its deity; the sixth is said to belong to Kubera;
the seventh has Soma as its deity, and the eighth has all the gods as its deity.
That which is the ninth from the front is known as the "Great Earth" (mahat pārthiva);
it should be made with cow dung and soaked overnight in water.
They say that the distance from one mandala to the next is thirty-two finger-breadths;
however, the mandala should be made according to the measure of the performer's own even footstep.
[1.8.7 The Procedure for Water] From the point where an arrow was discharged, a youth endowed with speed should go with his utmost strength to where that middle arrow has fallen.
Taking up a middle-range arrow, another man of similar description should return with speed from the direction where that first man has gone.
"But when the one who has come to take the arrow does not clearly see [the object] within the water, then one should declare him pure."
When the middle arrow has been drawn back, one whose body is submerged [in water] attains purity;
otherwise, one is not purified even if only a single limb is seen [above the water].
Or, from the place where he first discharged it, by moving elsewhere, [he attains purity].
Having caused the man to enter the water, one should discharge three arrows;
a wise man should not release the arrows while the wind is blowing violently.
On uneven ground crowded with trees and stumps,
if a person has digested poison provided by the accuser without the use of mantras or medicinal herbs,
he shall be considered innocent; otherwise, however, he shall be punished and made to pay that wealth.
If, within seven days or even fourteen days, there is no loss of his sons, wife, or wealth, he shall be pure; of this there is no doubt.
[1.8.8 The Procedure for the Vessel] Whatever food the accused person has eaten, that very same circle of weapons should be washed and made him drink three handfuls of that water.
The king should cause [the goods] to be moved through that place under the supervision of his own men for three or five nights, keeping it under surveillance due to the suspicion of trickery.

In cases of a great accusation, against one who is devoid of virtue, an ungrateful person, a eunuch, a contemptible person, an atheist, or one whose guilt has been previously observed, one should administer the ordeal of drinking from the sacred vessel (*kośapāna*).
One should always avoid divine ordeals for men afflicted by diseases; however,
one may administer the ordeal of rice (*taṇḍula*) for those among the subjects who suffer from diseases of the mouth.
During a solar eclipse, one who observes the fast, being pure, should eat rice grains;
he shall become purified by vomiting white [rice], but if it is otherwise, he incurs guilt.
Where blood is seen, and where the jaw and palate shatter,
and whose body trembles— one should declare such a person impure.
[1.8.10 The Procedure for the Heated Māṣa Coin] He should extract a heated māṣa coin from well-heated oil or ghee,
while summoning the truth with his thumb and finger joined, free from fear.
Having taken cow's ghee in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay, one who is pure should heat it over a fire.
One should cast into that [water] a very beautiful ring made of gold, silver, copper, or iron,
which has been washed once with water.
In a place rich with whirling whirlpools and waves, which is beyond the reach of the touch of a fingernail,
one should examine the presence of a *caruka* (a sacrificial oblation) by means of a moist leaf, noting whether it produces a sound.
Then, one should consecrate that [clarified butter] once with this mantra:
"O clarified butter, you are the supreme purifier, the nectar in sacrificial rites."
"O Purifier, burn away my sin; be cool as snow and pure!
Then, having fasted and bathed, he approaches wearing wet clothes."
One should have her take that very seal-ring while it is placed in the midst of clarified butter.
Then the examiners should examine his index finger;
if it does not cause the tip of the hand to tremble or if no blister arises,
he is pure according to the law, just as the word of Pitāmaha declares.
[1.8.11 The Procedure for the Ploughshare Test] A forged iron ploughshare weighing twelve palas is said [to be the instrument].
If it remains unburnt, one shall attain purification; otherwise, however, one is defeated.

It should be eight finger-breadths long and four finger-breadths wide; if the thief licks it with his tongue once while it is glowing like fire and is not burned, he attains purification; otherwise, he is defeated.
The members of the court must diligently provide a ploughshare for the field;
these [ordeals] are to be used in major charges when the accuser has placed his head [as a stake].
[1.8.12 The Ritual for the Dharmaka] On two leaves, one should write *dharma* and *adharma* in white and black [ink].
[This is done] with mantras such as the "gift of life" (*jīvadāna*) and with *sāman* chants such as the *gāyatrī*.
Having addressed [the deity], one should worship with perfumes and white and black flowers;
then, having sprinkled [the area] with the five products of the cow, [the two images] are enclosed within lumps of clay.
Having made those two equal and placed them in the jar unobserved,
he should then take one lump from the jar without delay.
If *dharma* is upheld, he shall be pure and honored by the examiners;
but if *adharma* is upheld, he shall be punished or even banished.
One should write down *dharma* and *adharma* as white and black, respectively, upon a birch-bark scroll.
Having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow, one should worship it with perfumes and garlands.
Dharma is white-flowered, while adharma is that which bears black flowers;
having prepared them in this manner and anointed them, one should cause those two lumps to be held.
Then, two equal lumps should be made either of cow dung or of clay;
they should be placed in an undamaged clay vessel and kept out of sight.
Having smeared a clean place and being in the presence of the gods and Brahmins,
he should then worship the gods and the world-protectors as before.
But preceded by the invocation of Dharma, one should write the document of the claim:
"If I am free from sin, may Dharma come into my hand."
Of those two [the scales], the accused shall grasp one without delay;
if the scale of truth is grasped, there shall be purity, but if it is the scale of untruth, he shall perish.
Reflecting in this manner, the king does not fall away from righteousness or worldly prosperity.

[1.9. The Manner of Decision] [1.9.0] Decision regarding a doubtful matter is declared to be of four kinds: by means of dharma, by means of legal procedure (vyavahāra), by means of conduct (cāritra), and by means of the king’s command.
Each one is declared by the wise to be of two kinds according to the distinction of action;
and one should determine the punishment in accordance with the offense.
Having thoroughly investigated the matter and determined it through reasoning,
and having tested it by means of oaths— that is to be known as the final adjudication of the law.
Where the defendant admits [the claim], that is the legal decision;
when it has been properly cleared by ordeals, it is declared to be a correct decision.
That legal proceeding which is determined by the means of valid knowledge is called the first; the second is proclaimed as that which lacks a reply due to quibbling over words (*vākchala*).
Conduct determined by inference is so described;
however, the third [type] is cited by those learned in the scriptures as being established by local custom.
But when the evidence is equal, it is traditionally held that the king's command is the final decision;
this is proclaimed as the fourth [type of decision], provided it does not contradict the scriptures or the members of the court.
But when there is a conflict with the Dharmaśāstras, a rule that is supported by reason is declared [authoritative].
Except for execution, there is never any punishment for a Brāhmaṇa;
"Brāhmaṇas and cows are not to be killed in this world"—this is the Vedic tradition.
Even if he is guilty of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), a Brahmin does not deserve corporal punishment;
the king should instead impose banishment, branding, and shaving his head.
And those who have committed great offenses, he should punish with the death penalty.
For a very slight offense, there shall be punishment by word or the "fie" punishment; for the first degree of violence, the same;
but for the middle and highest degrees, half the fine is prescribed, as well as imprisonment for treason against the king.

One who desires his own welfare should carry out either banishment or even execution for a perpetrator of a great sin (mahāpātaka), whether these measures are applied individually or collectively against a single offender.
One should employ verbal punishment against friends and others, saying, "Shame on these wretched men!
And one should also punish with fines those men who are litigious or hostile toward wealth.
Neither father, teacher, friend, mother, wife, son, nor domestic priest—
none who has deviated from his own duty is exempt from punishment by the king.
Sacrificial priests, domestic chaplains, ministers, sons, kinsmen,
and relatives who deviate from the dharma shall be punished by kings and banished from the city.
One should punish teachers, domestic priests, and those worthy of honor solely with the "staff of speech";
other litigants, however, one should punish with "reproach" and fines.
Likewise, those born in the inverse order of castes and the lowest classes are declared to be the dregs of men;
when they commit an offense against a Brāhmaṇa, they are to be executed and never to be made to pay a fine.
A man deserving of death shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred suvarṇas;
one deserving of the amputation of a limb shall pay half of that, and one deserving of a cut on the ear shall pay half of that again.
Beating, imprisonment, and likewise the provision of coarse food—this indeed is the punishment for a Śūdra; Bṛhaspati says there is no monetary fine.
One is declared a victor in the world by virtue of establishing one's thesis through cultivation, by honoring the judge and others, and by the issuance of a certificate of victory.

The defeat of the inferior party is incurred through fleeing, by not providing a reply, or by resorting to the side of the opponent; it does not occur for one who has been defeated by their own statements.
Even when the facts have been determined by the family and others, if the defendant is not satisfied,
the king, after investigating the matter, shall set aside that wrongful judgment and retry the case.
Having reached a decision together with many Brahmins who have mastered the scriptures,
he should punish the former members of the court along with the victorious party if they are found guilty.
And in this case, a punishment corresponding to the offense has been prescribed;
[the defendant] is defeated by means of witnesses, documents, inference, or properly by ordeal.
He who does not pay the prescribed fine for what is due shall be banished from that city.
For a Brāhmaṇa, no punishment other than branding on the forehead is ordained;
even if he is guilty of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), a Brāhmaṇa does not deserve the death penalty. The king should impose banishment, branding, and shaving of the head.
Whatever authority has been granted by him regarding all matters of gain, loss, expenditure, and income—
whether in his own country or abroad— that independence shall not be contradicted.

He who, having been appointed by his master to manage wealth, is entrusted with the authority to engage in money-lending, agriculture, and trade, is known as a *nisṛṣṭārtha* (an agent with full discretionary power).
The king must diligently investigate matters that are doubtful;
in doing so, three parties are benefited while the loss falls upon one alone.
The victor obtains wealth and honor; the defeated receives discipline and restraint.
The king attains victory, charity, and self-control, while the members of the court obtain merit.
Thus, by performing the adjudication and protection ordained in the scriptures, a king,
having spread his fame throughout this world, shall become equal to Mahendra.
By resolving legal cases through witnesses, written documents, and inference,
a king spreads his fame here on earth and attains the realm of the Sun.
Wherever a king thus understands the sacrificial decision,
he attains fame in this world and goes to the same realm as Śakra.
[1.10 Non-payment of Debt] This legal procedure has been proclaimed together with its subdivisions. Now hear the sections concerning other causes of dispute.

I shall explain in due order, according to their true nature, the principal matters concerning the non-payment of debt, as well as gambling and betting, along with the various types of legal procedures involved.
That which is debt to be paid and that which is not to be paid, by whom, where, and in what manner,
as well as the rules for giving and receiving— this is declared in the legal tradition to be the law concerning the non-payment of debt.
[1.10.1 Consideration of Interest] The interest shall be one-eightieth part [per month] when there is security;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be two, three, four, or five percent per month.
Having received the pledge or the collateral in its entirety along with reliable witnesses,
the creditor shall always deliver the debt recorded in writing or witnessed by others.
From one who is contemptible and from one who is in distress, money is taken by those free from hesitation;
therefore, that which is called usury is traditionally held to be fourfold or eightfold [the principal].
In the Purāṇa, the interest is one paṇa;
it is declared to be fourfold by some, and proclaimed as fivefold by others.
These have been declared by others to be of six kinds; understand them according to their true nature.
Interest on the body, interest for a fixed time, and the wheel-interest which is other than these;
likewise, stipulated interest, crest-interest, and profit from use.
Interest connected with bodily labor may be collected monthly;
likewise, interest that accrues over time, compound interest, and interest stipulated by the debtor himself.
That interest which is collected daily is known as *śikhā-vṛddhi*.
It grows constantly like a topknot, but it ceases upon the cutting off of the head.
But that interest which has been stipulated by the debtor himself as being excessive,
if it was agreed upon during a time of distress, must always be paid as contracted.
Interest stipulated otherwise must not be paid under any circumstances whatsoever.
Like a crest-lock, it grows constantly until it ceases upon the severing of the head;
likewise, when the root is provided, this growth of the crest-lock continues—thus it is remembered.
The house, the threshing floor, and the field are declared to be the acquisitions of enjoyment.
They say there are four kinds of interest: corporeal, interest on use, stipulated interest, and that which consists of the crest-lock; with compound interest as the fifth.
The creditor may collect interest, bodily labor, and likewise the profit from the use of the property,
only so long as the principal has not been repaid.
[1.10.3 Interest on Gold, Grain, and Other Goods] Interest on gold becomes double; on clothing and base metals, it is triple;
and on grain, as well as on fodder, beasts of burden, and wool, it is declared to be fourfold.
In the case of potherbs, the fivefold interest has been stated; for seeds and grain, it is traditionally held to be sixfold.
For salt, sweat-products, and fresh foods, an eightfold increase is considered appropriate. This same rate is declared for molasses and honey when they have been kept for a long time.
The interest on all kinds of oils, liquors, honey, clarified butter,
molasses, and salt is declared to be eightfold.
The profit on precious stones shall be fivefold; on cotton, fourfold;
and on wood such as sandalwood and the like, the increase shall be eightfold.
If a share [of interest] is taken that exceeds double the principal, or if compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*) is collected,
or if the debt is paid with interest only after the full term has expired, that usury is censured.
The eightieth part [of the principal] shall increase until the profit reaches double the principal;
this occurs without doubt after seven years and three quarters.
In the case of grass, wood, bricks, thread, fermenting agents, leather, bone, armor,
weapons, flowers, and fruits, interest does not cease.
The interest on gold, grain, and cloth is two, three, and four times the principal respectively;
the interest on ghee is eightfold, and that on copper and other metals is fourfold.
The creditor may collect interest on the head, bodily interest, and likewise profit on the enjoyment [of collateral],
as long as the principal has not been cleared.
For the others, the punishment increases successively by one-quarter.
In all disputes concerning property, one who employs verbal quibbling does not fail;
even if he is to be punished in cases involving another's wife, land, or non-payment of debt, he does not lose his claim.
One should always maintain equal interest; however, if it is unequal, it ceases.
[1.10.4 Interest on Wealth] Listen to the interest rates for usurers as declared in the words of Vasiṣṭha:
five *māṣas* for every twenty [units of currency]; in this way, the Dharma is not violated.
A māṣa is declared to be one-twentieth part of a pala.
But in that case, whatever man shows indifference toward this [matter],
a fine of four suvarṇas and six niṣkas is ordained for him.
Whatever one may obtain for the sake of accomplishing the business of a corporation, or upon an audience with the king and other such authorities,
that shall be shared equally among all members.
Likewise, for those such as heirs and others, this is their eternal law:
that a debt which was acquired with effort, or preserved, or contracted for the sake of the community [must be paid].
[1.10.5 Interest Not Contracted] Even if he resides in his own country, if one who has been repeatedly requested does not pay,
he shall pay the interest as it was caused to accrue there, even if he is unwilling.
Whether it be a six-monthly or a monthly debt, it should be divided according to their respective shares;
or it may be paid to those who are destitute, the elderly, the afflicted, women, children, the infirm, and the sick.
After three seasons, one may recover the principal along with interest;
in such cases as these, an eightieth part [of the principal] is intended as the rate of interest.
That which does not flow out [as interest] shall be the principal portion for the creditor;
even when doubled, there is no further increase for that which is subject to periodic interest (*kālika*).
Then the king should decide [the case] through those who know the true principles of legal procedure and dispute.
[1.10.6 Adhi] But a pledge is used for as long as it has not been returned.
A pledge (ādhi) is defined as a bond (bandha), and it is said to be of four kinds:
movable and immovable, as well as that which is to be guarded (gopya) and that which is to be enjoyed (bhogya).
A debt that is voluntary, has a fixed term, is recorded in writing,
and is witnessed, as well as one where the profit is not yet settled, may be recovered by the creditor once the term has expired.
He who, out of greed, consumes a pledge shall not receive the interest again;
it must be preserved like a deposit, for the interest is lost if it is consumed.
If a pledge should be destroyed due to an act of God or by the king, the debtor shall cause another pledge to be given; otherwise, he shall pay the debt along with the interest.
Whatever may be owed by one who has been placed under arrest, whether by means of a public proclamation or through his conduct,
if the debt is not paid, the debtor shall never be made to pay the full amount of the fine for detention against his will.
If the pledged object has been used until it reaches a state of worthlessness, the loss of the principal occurs;
in that case, whatever was of great value is lost, and the debtor should satisfy the creditor.
When a single field has been given as a pledge to two parties at the same time,
whoever has possessed it first shall obtain its legal title.
If two [claims] arise at the same time, the [liability] shall be equal for both;
this very rule is proclaimed to apply to both gifting and sale.
When a mortgage, sale, or gift has been executed by means of a document containing witnesses,
a document that contradicts it through a single act of transaction is considered a forgery.
Kātyāyana declared that an unspecified document, one that has been specified, and one that is qualified in a single place— among these, the one written with specific qualifications is superior.
When the interest on gold has doubled and the stipulated time has expired,
the creditor becomes the owner of the pledge after waiting for twelve days.
If the debtor provides money within that interval, he may recover the pledge;
once the stipulated period has expired and the interest has been fully realized, the owner of the pledge shall then become its master.
However, if ten days have not yet elapsed, the debtor is entitled to redeem it.
When a pledge for custody has reached twice its value, or when the stipulated time has expired according to the rule,
it shall immediately be announced in the debtor's family and may then be used [by the creditor].
When the gold has doubled in interest and the debtor is still unable to pay,
the creditor shall seize the debtor's property and sell it in the presence of witnesses.
Or, having fixed a price, he should keep it for ten days in the presence of the public;
thereafter, having received a deposit corresponding to its value, he should relinquish it to another.
If a debtor does not enjoy his own pledge, nor deliver it, nor announce it [to others],
and if the witness has died, the creditor's written document is rendered useless.
A house, a field, a shop, grain, livestock, women, and vehicles— these perish through neglect and likewise fall into a state of worthlessness.
Having secured his own wealth with men skilled in accounting,
and having it witnessed by the kinsmen and relatives of the debtor, he may take possession of it without incurring offense.
The eighteen-fold dispute, distinguished by its plaint and reply, has been explained; now, however, understand correctly the various types of legal procedures.
An action that was previously performed must be maintained exactly as it was;
where it is performed otherwise, then there is a deviation in the action.
If, having first abandoned the instrument [of proof], either the creditor or the debtor should produce evidence that is deficient,
excessive, or inconsistent, that is called a "distortion of the legal procedure" (*kriyābheda*).
If one who has received two units of wealth for a loan subsequently admits to a profit of five units,
that latter amount which is definitively established shall be the authority regarding the interest thereon.
But that gift or sale which is made by one who is not the owner is to be known as invalid; such is the established rule in legal proceedings.
By each successive bond, the preceding bond becomes loosened;
that which is the final act of performance is more powerful than the prior one.
Whether one has made a deposit or established a pledge elsewhere, yet subsequently establishes a pledge [with another],
or sells it— if such an action occurs, the latter transaction is the stronger.
If a sale, a mortgage, and a gift are all made on the same day,
and it is uncertain which of the three occurred first, how should the matter be adjudicated?
In this case, there are exactly three authorities; they should divide [the property] according to their respective shares.
Both [the father and the mother] shall do so in accordance with the purpose, and the recipient shall take a third part.
If the debt has been paid in full and the land has been cultivated, then the owner of the wealth shall not receive his share,
nor shall the debtor recover his pledge, except by mutual agreement.
If a debtor, having paid the principal amount of the loan, requests the release of the pledge, it must be released to him at that very time; otherwise, the creditor becomes liable for the offense.
When land or other property has been enjoyed [by the creditor], and the profit derived from it exceeds the principal,
such that the interest has entered into the principal, then the debtor shall recover the pledge.
If the creditor is absent, the debtor shall deposit the money as a pledge with a third party and take possession of the property.
When the debtor, having made a formal agreement, gives the field to the creditor, it is settled that the property must be released once the interest on that capital has been fully paid.
"But the pledge must be returned to me when the principal has yielded its profit;
this is declared to be the righteous rule regarding the law of usury and pledges."
Where a house or field has been held for a long time through possession and has become superior [in value],
there the debtor shall recover the pledge and the creditor likewise his debt.
When the excellence is complete, that equality of both is proclaimed;
but when it is incomplete, the two should act according to each other's consent.
If that [debt] has been fully discharged, then the creditor is no longer entitled to the wealth;
the debtor does not forfeit his pledge without the mutual consent of both parties.
Surety] In the treatises, wise men have observed four types of surety: for appearance, for confidence, for payment, and likewise for the delivery of the debtor's property.
One says, "I shall show it," while another virtuous person says, "I am the giver; let this wealth be bestowed. Another might say, "Let me be the one to bestow it."
But a surety for appearance who produces [the debtor] in the proper place and time,
or brings forward the security, shall not be liable therefor, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
The creditor shall grant time for the recovery of lost property to the surety;
this period may be a fortnight, a month, or even half a month, depending on the distance, the route, and the nature of the object.
If a man stands as a surety for another's appearance here,
failing to produce him, he shall pay that debt to the creditor from his own wealth.

If the first two [witnesses] prove to be false, they shall be made to pay the wealth as it was known at that time; but if the latter two disagree, they shall be punished, as shall their sons in their absence.

The owner, one imprisoned by an enemy, an official, one punished, those under suspicion, an heir, a friend, an outcaste, a resident pupil, one who has served a king, an ascetic, a religious student, a pauper, a child, an elderly person, a woman, and one afflicted by illness are not eligible to stand as sureties.
If the person for whom bail was posted fails to appear, the surety must pay the amount again.

A debt incurred by a father must be paid in its entirety even by his son. However, if one who has been pressured by the debtor pays what was guaranteed as bail, he may seek reimbursement from that debtor.
After three fortnights, he is entitled to recover his property along with double the profit.
If, because they are simple-minded, those who have not been educated should pay a debt merely out of a sense of propriety,
they shall by no means recover from that person the wealth for which they were made to pay.
They should not be subjected to excessive hardship; rather, they should be made to pay the debt gradually.
They should not be compelled to act as witnesses for themselves; this is the rule regarding sureties.
When the debtor has disappeared or died, the creditor shall present the document and cause a new deed of location to be executed, specifying the time limit for its validity.
But when money has been paid by a surety to the creditor without being authorized to do so,
it shall not be made double and returned to the surety by the debtor.

A debtor who has admitted a debt may be compelled to pay it through conciliatory means such as persuasion, as well as by means of religious pressure, deception, force, or confinement in the house. BP1.10.087c/dharma-upadhi-balāt-kāraiḥ gṛha-saṃrodhanena ca.

Through the mediation of friends and relatives, by means of conciliatory speech, and by following [the debtor], the creditor should generally be made to pay; this is declared to be the righteous course.
But a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished should be made to pay gradually, according to his income. When a creditor, having brought from the debtor money that was requested under a pretext,
or having recovered a deposit or the like, causes the debt to be paid there, it is considered a fraudulent transaction (*sa-upadhi*).
When a debtor is brought to his own house and compelled by force through methods such as beating and the like to pay, that is declared to be *balāt-kāra* (coercion).
Even by means of labor, the debtor may make himself equal to the creditor;
likewise, one of equal or lower caste should pay what remains, but that gradually.

One may compel a person of low caste who has become destitute to perform labor for the sake of repaying a debt; however, a Brāhmaṇa who is destitute should be made to pay gradually, according to his income.
When a debtor is made to pay his own wealth by binding his wife, children, and cattle, or by sitting at his own door, that is called *ācarita* (customary practice).
This rule applies to one who has admitted his debt; however, if he denies it in court, he is compelled to pay after being made to prove his claim by means of a document or witnesses.
"I shall give that which is rightfully to be given"—
when a debtor speaks thus, he is called one who asserts his legal claim (*kriyāvādī*).
One who asserts a legal claim regarding a doubtful matter must never be obstructed in any way.
However, he who restrains one who should not be restrained is liable to punishment according to the law.

When there is a confusion between two parties regarding form, number, and so forth, or concerning gains, or even when the matter of what should be given and what should not be given is doubtful— that is declared to be a "doubtful case."
When the stipulated period has expired and the interest has ceased to accrue, the creditor shall recover the debt,
or the debtor may retain the document under an arrangement for compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*).
When compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*) is stipulated at more than double the principal,
then the profit from the use of the property (*bhogalābha*) shall constitute the principal with interest for the creditors.
But he who proceeds with a doubtful matter without having informed the king shall be punished by force, and that legal matter shall not be established.
Now it is stated what debt, having been received from another's hand according to the rules of usury,
must be repaid by whom, where, and how, and what may not be repaid.
A debt contracted for a short period must be repaid when requested;
once the deadline has expired, it must be paid with interest at peace, even by sons in the absence of the father.
If an ascetic who maintains the sacred fires dies while still indebted,
both his ascetic merit and his fire-sacrifice shall all belong to the owner of the debt.
If a debtor has no wealth, the creditor shall bring him to his house and compel him to work;
however, a Brāhmaṇa who is a drunkard or of similar character shall be made to pay the debt gradually.
Among those who take the wealth, the wife, or the son [of a deceased person], the liability for debt follows in order according to their precedence.
In their absence, it goes to the others who are heirs in due order.

Debts to be Paid] A debt must be recorded from the outset in accordance with the law; however, if one does not record it subsequently, nor indeed pay what has been admitted, he shall incur interest on that amount.
In the case of those who are diseased, insane, aged, or likewise long absent,
one should cause such a debt to be paid by their sons, even while they are still living.
Even while the father is present, the debt must be paid by the sons once it has been proven;
this applies even in the case of those who are born blind, outcastes, insane, or afflicted with consumption, leprosy, and similar diseases.
Among those who have entered under a single title of ownership, he who is seen there shall be made to pay;
however, the son of one who has gone abroad shall receive the entire paternal share upon that father's death.
If the father has been sent away, the son shall pay the entire debt incurred under a single family obligation;
however, when the father is dead, he shall pay only his paternal share, and never more than that for the father's debts.
The debt of the father must first be paid, and then one's own;
of those two, the grandfather’s debt must be paid first—thus always should a debt be settled.

A debt incurred by a father must be paid by his sons once it has been proven, just as if it were their own; a debt incurred by a grandfather is to be paid equally [by the grandsons], but that which was incurred by him is not to be paid by the son.
Even one who is dependent may conduct legal business for the sake of the family, whether in his own country or abroad; a learned man should not obstruct such a transaction.
Therefore, once a son is born, he should strive diligently to release his father from debt by setting aside his own interests, so that the father does not go to hell.
When the father has passed away, the sons shall pay the debt according to their respective shares,
whether they are divided or undivided, or whoever may have undertaken that burden.

One should not compel a son to pay a gift made for the sake of the sun or for the sake of dice, a gift given in vain, that promised out of lust or anger, a suretyship obligation, or the remainder of a fine or a tax.
The manager of the wives of liquor-sellers, hunters, washermen, cowherds, barbers,
and boatmen shall be made to pay their debts incurred in the business of their husbands.
If a son who inherits the debt and the property is also a source of trouble, he shall likewise be the one to take the wife; this applies in the absence of an heir to the wealth.
What has been borrowed for the sake of the family by a paternal uncle, a brother’s son, a wife, a slave, a pupil, or a dependent, that the householder ought to repay.

He who is appointed by his master to oversee income and expenditure, or is entrusted with funds for lending at interest, agriculture, or trade, is known as a *nisṛṣṭārtha* (an agent with full discretionary power).
"He who, having taken items such as a loan for use, does not return them to the owner,
is born as that person's slave, son, wife, or livestock in his house."
A debt incurred by a son must be cleared by the father if it was approved by him; or, out of affection for his son, he may pay it himself, but he is not otherwise obligated to do so.
The debtor shall recover his pledge after the full term has expired by paying the principal amount together with the interest, provided the pledge was intended for the enjoyment of its fruits.
If that [loan] has been repaid in full, then the creditor shall not be entitled to the wealth,
nor shall the debtor be liable for the pledge, except by mutual agreement.
If a debtor who owes a lower debt is summoned by a creditor for the purpose of recovering a higher debt,
the judge shall cause him to pay the amount of the lower debt as proven to the creditor.
But one who denies a debt, yet is proven by evidence,
shall be made to pay the creditor’s claim and a fine according to his ability.
Whatever amount of wealth one may conceal, or whatever amount one may falsely claim in a lawsuit—
both of them, being ignorant of righteousness, shall be made by the king to pay a fine double that amount.
If one has received money on account of a lawful debt or similar grounds, but does not cause it to be recorded in writing,
nor pays the amount when it is due for payment, that sum shall accrue interest for him.
[1.11 Deposits] The taking of loans, beginning with the lending and ending with the repayment, has been proclaimed.
Now, let the proper procedure for deposits be heard.
That which is given without being described, separated [from witnesses], uncounted, not shown,
and marked with a seal, is known as *upanidhi* (a sealed deposit).

[1.11.2 The Nature of Deposit (*nyāsa*)] When property is placed in another's house out of fear of kings, thieves, or enemies, or due to deception regarding the receipt of inheritance— that is proclaimed to be a deposit (*nyāsa*).

[1.11.3 The Method of Concealment] One should conceal the treasure after considering the location, the house, the site itself, the various qualities of that debt, as well as truthfulness, purity, and kinsmen.
[1.11.4 Its Twofold Nature] Furthermore, that [non-apprehension] is said to be of two kinds: that which possesses a witness and the other [which does not].
Likewise, its confirmation consists in the restoration [of the object], or else there would be a contrary conviction [in the case of its absence].
It is declared to be of two kinds: that witnessed by witnesses and that given in secret.
It must be protected like a son; otherwise, it perishes through neglect.
Whatever merit there may be for one who gives gold, base metals, garments, and so forth, that same merit belongs to one who protects a deposit,
as well as one who has come for refuge.
Just as there is no fault for a noble woman in betraying her husband, nor for a man in killing his son or friend,
so too there is no fault for men in consuming or neglecting a deposit.
One should not take possession of property placed in trust; its loss brings dishonor.
What has been accepted should be protected with care, and it should be returned when requested even once.

Whatever was deposited according to which procedure, and by whom it was proven to belong to another, that must be returned to him exactly as it was; otherwise, it is not to be given back, except for the immediate next-of-kin.
[1.11.6 Rules regarding the loss of a deposit] If that [deposit] should meet its destruction due to an act of God or the king,
there is no fault in that case, provided it is returned together with the property of the borrower.
If the borrower, having received a deposit with its specific characteristics and with the understanding that it may be neglected, should destroy it,
or if he should not return it when asked for, he shall be compelled to pay it back along with interest.

[1.11.7 Punishment for Misuse of Deposits] Whoever should accomplish his own business by means of another's deposited property shall be punished by the king and made to pay that property along with interest.
[1.11.8 Decision on Denial] If a person, having received a deposit, denies it, he shall be made to prove its existence through witnesses or by oath;
once proven, he must be made to restore the deposit along with an equal fine as a penalty.
When a dispute arises regarding a secret deposit that was delivered in private,
it is ordained by the legal tradition that an ordeal shall serve as the means of proof for both parties.
If a gift has been made privately by someone, or accepted privately, it must be returned privately; as the giving was, so too must be the taking back.
One shall not incur any liability in the case of an ocean, provided one does not take anything from it;
this same rule applies to what has been placed for safekeeping, what has been borrowed, the deposit of an artisan, a pledge, and likewise for one who has come for refuge.
If a deposit is being refined over a fixed number of days,
and the artisan keeps it beyond that period, he must pay for it even if it was destroyed by an act of God.
One who gives back what was requested with the owner’s permission shall not be at fault.
[This concludes the section on "Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner.
Immediately following the topic of deposits, Bhṛgu has declared the section on "Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner."
Listen to that with diligence; I shall explain it to you in detail.
[1.12.1 Definition of One Who Is Not the Owner] One who takes a deposit, a loan for use, a sealed deposit, what has been stolen, what has been asked for, or a pledge;
or one who sells in secret or before a crowd— he is declared to be "one who is not the owner."
[1.12.2 Fault in Purchase from One Not Announced to the Superintendent] But for one who purchases at a price after having previously announced it to the superintendent,
no fault exists; there would be no thief because of the purchase made under a pretext.
[1.12.3 The Definition of Upavikraya (Selling at a Loss)] That which is purchased inside a house or outside a village at night from an absent person,
or for a low price, is to be known as *upavikraya*.
[1.12.4 Determination of the Purity of the Purchaser] But if the former owner, having arrived, should investigate that property,
the price must be shown; from that, the purity of the purchaser shall be established.
When the original source has been recovered, the purchaser is not to be prosecuted in any way;
however, the dispute regarding the price is not lost to the owner of the eightfold property.
Where the seller is produced [as a witness], the purchaser shall lose his case in the legal proceeding;
he must pay the price and a fine to the king, and the value of the property to the owner.
He who, devoid of ownership and driven by greed, covets another's property,
and subsequently fails to relinquish it, shall be compelled to pay a fine double the value of that property.
But in a legal proceeding where the evidence is deficient,
the king himself should make the decision based on the status of the individuals involved, according to whether they are equal, inferior, or superior.

Where goods have passed through a merchant's stall, or are known by royal officers, or were purchased from an unknown source, or where the seller is dead; [in such cases, the purchaser must prove his innocence].
The owner, having paid half the value, shall take back his own property; in that case, half of the stolen goods shall belong to both parties according to legal procedure.
Purchasing without proper examination and likewise failing to provide protection—
these two have been declared by the Buddhas to be causes of the loss of property.
If an article found in a merchant's row has been identified by royal officers and seized during the day, a wealthy purchaser acquires that property as his own.
But if, after selling land, one does not provide the purchaser with possession, he shall restore that property to him; otherwise, he incurs the punishment of a thief.
These two have been declared by the wise to be causes of loss of property:
that in which no value can be determined because the specific characteristics are unknown.
In that case, the loss shall be considered equal for both the purchaser and the one who denies the ownership.
[1.13 Collective Undertaking] [1.13.1 Those Authorized to Act Collectively] (p.
129) BP1.13.001a/ By those who are of noble birth, capable, untiring, wise, and knowledgeable in coinage;
One should carry out activities together with those who know income and expenditure, who are pure, and who are brave.
Whatever the share of anyone may be— whether equal, greater, or less— in that case,
their loss, expenditure, and increase shall be of that same kind.
[1.13.2 Those Unqualified] Wise men should not engage in activities such as trade and the like with those who are incapable, lazy, afflicted by disease, unfortunate, or without support.
[1.13.3 Profit according to the nature of the commodity:
But for those who carry out an investment with gold, grain, liquids, and so forth,
their profit shall be of a corresponding kind, according to shares that are equal, less, or more.
Whether a share is equal, less, or more than what was assigned, it shall be exactly so;
for he shall bear the loss, perform the work, and likewise receive the profit.
[1.13.4 Determination in those debates] Those very same persons are declared to be both examiners and witnesses for one another regarding a doubtful matter,
provided they are not motivated by deceit or possessed by mutual hatred.
If anyone among them is recognized as a cheat in buying or selling, he shall be cleared by means of oaths; this rule applies in all disputes concerning transactions.
[1.13.5 Decision regarding Loss of Property] When a loss of property occurs therein due to acts of fate or the king,
that loss is declared to belong to all [the partners]; it should be apportioned accordingly according to their shares.
If, however, one who was not specifically assigned the task loses the property through negligence while it is being sought, he alone must restore it;
that debt shall be borne by all the partners equally.
Having given a sixth part to the king, they shall receive [the remainder] according to their respective shares.

[1.13.6 The Protector’s Tenth Share] Out of fear of divine or royal calamities, he should protect [the people] to the best of his ability. Having given him a tenth share, they may take the remainder from that portion.
[1.13.7 Customs Duties] When a merchant arrives at a customs station, he shall pay the duty as is appropriate. He must not deviate from that; this is proclaimed as the tribute due to kings.
This is not the case when a calamity caused by thieves, the king, or fire has occurred;
however, for one who protects [the property] according to his own ability, a tenth part is prescribed as his share.
[1.13.8 Decision regarding the loss of one among those performing joint labor: When a certain merchant there should die through negligence,
his merchandise must be displayed by the appointed royal officers.
When someone should appear at that time, that man who is the heir to the estate must prove his ownership by means of other [means of proof]; only then is he entitled to receive it.
The king should take a sixth, a ninth, or likewise a tenth part from those of the Śūdra, Vaiśya, and Kṣatriya castes; however, he should take a twentieth part from the Brāhmaṇa.
But if the owner does not come forward in any way after three years, then the king may take that property; however, he must entrust the property belonging to a Brāhmaṇa to other Brāhmaṇas.
Thus, when anyone among those engaged in a ritual action passes away,
that action must be performed by his kinsman together with all the other participants.
[1.13.9 The Priests] The Adhvaryu shall take the chariot, and the Brahman the horse at the establishment of the fires;
the Hotṛ the horse that chooses the *nivid*, and the Udgātṛ the cart at the purchase [of the Soma].
Of all [the sons], the principal ones are entitled to half; others are entitled to half of that;
those entitled to a third receive a third share, and those entitled to a fourth receive a fourth share.
Those who arrive as guests, those who have come by succession, and likewise those who are self-appointed—these are declared to be of three kinds; one should conduct oneself toward them accordingly.
[1.13.10 The Manner of Joint Undertaking] If one man among many, being agreed upon by all, should give wealth or cause work to be done, it shall be considered as performed by all.

A debt incurred by kinsmen, relatives, or friends must be paid back even if it is secured by a pledge; likewise, the debts of others must be paid when they are accompanied by a mortgage, a written document, or witnesses.
Gold may be taken at one's own will; however, liquids and grain must be given with a time limit. They should be given and likewise received in accordance with local custom.
But that which is given by those assembled together must likewise be requested [back] by them;
and whoever does not ask for it is deprived of his share of the profit.
[1.13.11 Collective Agricultural Work] Listen; this rule concerning farmers and others is now being stated.
A wise man should engage in agriculture together with those who are equal to him in terms of draft animals, laborers, seed, and other implements for the field.
Where loss of a field occurs due to the destruction of external seeds,
that [loss] must be made good by that very person to all those who live by agriculture.
One should carefully avoid a field that is on a mountain, near a city, or along a royal road; likewise, one should avoid land that is saline or infested with mice.
One who sows at the proper time in a field that is dug up, situated near water, well-watered, endowed with boundaries on all sides, and well-prepared, enjoys the fruit.
A wise farmer should not acquire for his own use an ox that is emaciated, too old, lowly, diseased, or fleeing; nor one that is one-eyed or lame. He should keep such an animal for external labor.
This ancient law has been fully declared for the *kīnāśas* (plowmen/artisans) [and craftsmen]:
regarding gold, base metals, threads, wood, stone, and leather;
But the one who performs the refinement, being skilled in the arts, is called an artisan by the wise.
Where goldsmiths and others perform their craft collectively,
they shall receive wages corresponding to their work according to their respective shares.
Teachers who are instructors, experts, and skilled craftsmen shall receive one,
two, three, or four shares respectively, according to their increasing proficiency.
For those who, acting together, construct a mansion, a temple, or even the furnishings for a righteous purpose,
the leader among them is entitled to two shares.
This very same rule has been declared by the virtuous as the law for dancers:
one who knows the *tāla* receives one and a half shares, while the singers receive equal shares.
[1.13.13 Division of the Gain of Thieves] But that which has been brought back from a foreign country by thieves at the command of their master—
having given a sixth part to the king, they shall divide it among themselves according to their respective shares.
Then the eldest shall take four shares; the hero’s son shall obtain one share;
but the capable one shall take two shares, while all the remaining sons shall have equal shares.
Thus has been fully declared the settlement for those who have risen together; now the rules regarding what is not to be given,
what is to be given, what has been given, and what has not been given shall be told.
Common property, sons, wives, and so forth; all one's wealth; a deposit;
what has been requested; and likewise what has been promised to another—these eight kinds of things are traditionally held to be not to be given away.
That which remains after providing for the food and clothing of one's family must be given away;
otherwise, like the taste of honey followed by poison, the fate of the giver shall be otherwise.
Whatever field is acquired from the seven types of gardens or from a house and field— whether inherited from a father or acquired by oneself— that which is intended for distribution must be given.
That which is given by one's own will, that which is acquired by oneself, a pledge according to the custom of pledges,
and what is received in marriage or inherited through lineage— in all these cases, there is no gift of the entire property.
That which is obtained as a dowry, inherited through succession, acquired by valor,
or given with the permission of the woman's kinsmen or her husband, shall attain validity when bestowed.
Except for one's entire property and house, whatever wealth remains for the maintenance of the family and other such purposes—that is one's own property to be given; otherwise, it shall not be given.
Whether divided or undivided, heirs have equal rights over immovable property;
for in all matters of giving, causing to be given, or selling, a single heir has no power.
Wages, that which is given out of satisfaction, the price for merchandise, the bride-price,
a gift to one who has rendered assistance, and that which is given through faith, favor, or affection— this is recorded as the eightfold *datta*.
A gift given to a Śūdra is considered equal [in merit] to the object; to a Vaiśya, it is remembered as being twice that;
a gift to a Kṣatriya is threefold, and to a Brāhmaṇa, it is remembered as sixfold.
For a *śrotriya*, the fine is one thousand; for a sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), it is double that;
for a teacher (*ācārya*), it should be known as threefold; and for those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), it is double that.
If the offense is committed against one’s own kinsman, the fine is one thousand; however, it is infinite if committed against an Agnihotrī.
Against a Soma-drinker, it is one hundred thousand; against a teacher of the Veda, it is infinite.

A woman should bestow her own property upon her female relatives, but she should avoid giving it to those who are not of her kin; in the absence of female relatives, however, she should give it to her male kinsmen, and in their absence, to the twice-born.
That which is given with the thought "after me" does not bring merit to a living being;
because it has not been truly given at that time, it shall accrue to the heir upon his death.
With those who are angry, joyful, intoxicated, afflicted, childish, insane, or tormented by fear;
with those who are drunk, very old, arrogant, deluded, or overwhelmed by the force of grief.

Likewise, that which is given by Nandas or Dattas is proclaimed as "not given" (adatta) by these authorities; so too is what is given with the desire for a reciprocal gain, or what is given to an unworthy recipient while suspecting them to be worthy.
If, however, the work is connected with unrighteousness, the owner shall recover that [payment];
likewise, one who enjoys what has not been given and one who gives what should not be given shall be punished.
[1.15 Abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā] [1.15.0]
The rules for those who have entered into service regarding what is not to be given and so forth have been declared;
now, having undertaken service, this first point is being stated.
But when one has undertaken service and yet does not perform it— this undertaking of non-service is called the legal head of dispute concerning "having undertaken [service]."
The non-payment of wages, and for that purpose, the disputes between the owner and the keeper, are dealt with in sequence; this constitutes the threefold classification of hired laborers.
However, it is described in many ways according to birth and action;
it is fourfold, caused by knowledge, discernment, desire, and wealth.
Furthermore, each one of these is subdivided according to the differences in their ritual applications.
The triple Veda is declared to be characterized by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman;
for the sake of that [Veda], one should perform the service of the teacher as enjoined.
Skill is said to be proficiency in the arts, such as the working of gold and silver, as well as dancing and so forth; having acquired that, one should perform service in the teacher's house.
He who enjoys another’s female slave should be known as one hired by a mare;
he must perform labor for her master, just like a man hired for his food.
It is taught that there are many types of those who carry wealth for another, as well as others who carry a share;
furthermore, the distinction between inferior, middling, and superior has been declared for all of them.
One who has been made to work for a day, a month, half a month, three months, six months,
or a year shall perform the labor as promised and receive what was agreed upon.
A hired servant is to be known as being of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior;
their wages shall be based on their work and determined according to their ability and devotion.
In this regard, the highest wage is for a soldier, the middle for a cultivator, and the lowest for a porter; such is the threefold classification of hired laborers.
The soldier is declared the highest; the farmer is the middle;
the burden-carrier is declared the lowest, as is the householder who performs domestic labor.
The wage for those who live by agriculture and cattle-rearing is recorded as being of two kinds:
from the grain produced and likewise from the milk; he shall receive it, of this there is no doubt.
For these four are declared to be performers of auspicious work:
the student (*śiṣya*), the resident pupil (*antevāsī*), the hired servant (*bhṛtaka*), and the laborer (*karmakara*).
But the remaining five types of slaves are partakers of the lowest kind of work.
Action is also said to be of two kinds: auspicious and inauspicious.
Unpleasant work is prescribed for a slave, while pleasant work is traditionally assigned to a laborer;
this includes cleaning the house, the door, impure places, the streets, and the refuse heaps.

Touching the limbs of one who has been grasped, touching the limbs of one who is impure from eating, the handling or discarding of feces and urine, and finally, attending upon a departing master by following behind with one's own body.
Unwholesome action is to be known as [the first type], and wholesome action is other than that.
From that point forward, he is to be called one protected by the favor of his master;
he becomes one whose food may be eaten and whose gifts may be accepted, being esteemed by the virtuous.
Until he has grasped the [teaching on] ignorance, the student should serve his teacher with diligence;
his conduct toward the teacher’s wives and likewise toward the teacher’s son should be the same.
Having returned from his studies and having presented the teacher's fee (*guru-dakṣiṇā*) to the teacher, he returns home; this is declared to be the conduct of a student.
In this case, the first group of four is not released from slavery except by the favor of the master; their servitude is hereditary.
That lowest of men who, being independent, sells himself as an equal [slave]—
he is the most contemptible of these, and even he is not released from slavery.
A female slave who has been married by a slave shall also attain the status of a slave;
for her husband is her master, since his own authority is dependent upon the master.
And those sons born of a female slave, whether by her husband or by another man—
if the progenitor is the owner, the master shall not compel the female slave to work.
[1.16 Non-payment of Wages] The plowman shall take either a third or a fifth part [of the crop].
One who is supported by food and fodder shall take a fifth part from the plow.
If he is not maintained by wages, he may take a third part from a field where the crop has grown.
A hired servant must not practice even the slightest deception toward his master;
he incurs a loss of wages, and from that, a legal dispute arises.
[1.16.1 Determination regarding the non-performance of work by a hired laborer] If a hired laborer,
being free from illness, should out of pride fail to perform the work as stipulated,
he shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas*, and his wages shall not be paid.
[1.16.2 Punishment for One Who Has Received Wages] When a hired laborer who has received wages does not perform the work,
if he is capable, he shall be made to pay a fine of double those wages.
One who has received wages but abandons his work shall pay double the amount.
[1.16.3 Punishment for one who has not received wages:
If wages have not been received, the employer shall be made to pay an equal amount; the tools and equipment must be protected by those who have been hired.
[1.16.4 Punishment for Failing to Fulfill a Promise] He who, having made a promise, does not perform it, should be compelled to do so even by force;
if he still does not perform that task, he shall incur a fine of twenty [paṇas].
He shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas*, and his wages shall not be paid.

[1.16.5 Absence of Liability for Wages] Whatever work, even if it is unwholesome, a hired servant performs when directed by his master, the master shall not be held liable for that in respect of the wages.
[1.16.6 Times when the herdsman is free from fault] In the event of an act of God, by the king, or by legal necessity, as well as in the case of a calamity befalling the kingdom,
if cattle are lost or killed, the herdsman is not at fault therein.

[1.16.7 The Master’s Rule Regarding Punishment] If a master, once the work has been performed, does not pay the wages to the laborer, he shall be compelled by the king to pay them, and a fine shall be imposed in proportion to the offense.
[1.16.8 Punishment for the Fault of the Herdsman] But if there is destruction [of the cattle] without fault on the part of the herdsman, a fine is prescribed for the herdsman:
twelve and a half paṇas, and the value of the property itself must be paid to the owner.
If she is ill, exhausted, distracted, or occupied with royal duties,
and yet does not come when invited, she is considered a "barren mare" (baḍabā) who is beyond reproach.
[1.16.9 Duties of the Master and the Herdsman] Likewise, one who has been hired for milk should receive the entire amount of its milk on the eighth day;
he shall deliver all of this... [as previously detailed].
If he does not exert himself, does not raise an alarm, and fails to inform the owner,
