the cowherd must bear the loss and pay a fine to the king.
He should protect [the pasture] from the danger of worms, thieves, tigers, caves, and dogs;
he should drive them away according to his ability, or report it to the owner within the distance of one *krośa*.
One should drive away the cattle from the standing crops; however, if they have fed upon them, a double fault occurs:
the owner shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], while the keeper deserves corporal punishment.
Furthermore, if the crop has been consumed down to the roots, the fine for the damage shall be equal to the value of the field.
[1.17 Transgression of Agreements] [1.17.0] This indeed has been fully described as the conduct between masters and servants;
now, learn in brief the rules regarding agreements.
[1.17.1 Establishing the True Brāhmaṇas and Their Duties] Having summoned learned brāhmaṇas who are knowers of Vedic lore, well-versed in the scriptures, and maintainers of the sacred fire-offering,
he should establish them there and provide for their livelihood.
The king should grant them house-sites with the right to collect taxes from them without interruption;
having recorded this in his own edicts, he should ensure they are exempted and made secure.

They shall perform the daily rites, the occasional rites, those for the fulfillment of desires, as well as those for pacification and for prosperity; likewise, they shall provide a definitive decision in matters of doubt regarding the ancient rituals.
[1.17.2 Performing Dharma-Deeds Collectively] However, for the sake of the village, guild, or corporation, a convention and the performance of an agreement should be made;
that [agreement] must be carried out in times of distress, and likewise in matters of dharma.
Fear of robbers and thieves and the resulting distress are declared to be common to all;
therefore, the remedy for them must be undertaken by everyone collectively, not by any single individual alone.
[1.17.3 Establishing Trust] Having first established mutual trust through a deposit, a written contract, or mediators, they should thereafter carry out their business affairs.
Those who are hostile, addicted to vices, as timid as rice stalks,
those who are neither fit nor unfit for appointment, the greedy, the very aged, and children should not be appointed as deliberators on affairs of state.
Those who are pure, knowers of the Veda and Dharma, skillful, self-controlled, of noble birth,
and proficient in all affairs— such persons of great excellence should be appointed.
Two, three, or five persons should be appointed who speak for the welfare of the community;
their word must be carried out by the village, guilds, corporations, and so forth.
[1.17.5 Samayakriyā] The restoration of assembly halls, water-stations, temples, ponds,
and parks; likewise, the performance of funeral rites for the destitute and the poor, and the act of providing travel provisions.
"The lineage and its cessation must be maintained by us according to our respective shares;
as for this document which has been written in this manner, it is a righteous legal compact."

Those who are capable must protect [the weak]; however, for one who is capable but acts deceitfully toward them, the punishment shall be the confiscation of all his property and banishment from the city.
In that case, whatever man causes a breach or shows indifference [regarding the sacred fire],
a fine of four suvarṇas and six niṣkas is ordained for him.
But he who injures common property, or reviles one learned in the three Vedas, or obstructs a formal agreement or a ritual act, shall be banished from that city.
One who inflicts wounds, a slanderer, a creator of dissension, as well as one who commits violence,
and one who hates a guild, a corporation, or the king, shall be swiftly banished from there.
The heads of families, guilds, and assemblies, as well as those residing in cities and fortresses,
shall impose verbal censure, fines, corporal punishment, or banishment upon evildoers.

The punishment and favor toward men that they have carried out according to their own duty must also be approved by the king, for they are traditionally considered to have been delegated with full authority.
When those who have become filled with hatred cause harm to one another,
or when a conflict arises among the assemblies involving their leaders,
then the king shall investigate the matter and establish them upon their proper course.
He who, being capable [of fulfilling his obligation], should fail to do so,
shall be punished with the confiscation of all his property and banishment from the city.
Those who, having formed a partnership, take away the king’s share by acting as one,
as well as merchants who flee, shall be made to pay eight times that amount.
Then, whatever he may obtain, that shall be shared equally among all;
it should be divided according to their respective shares, whether it be a monthly or a six-monthly portion.
Or it may be given to those who are destitute, aged, blind, women, children, the infirm, or the diseased; likewise to those seeking to establish a lineage and so forth—this is the eternal law.
That which has been acquired through efforts, or preserved for the sake of the corporation, or staked as a wager,
or obtained through the favor of the king— all that belongs equally to everyone.
[1.18 Residual Disputes Concerning Purchase and Sale] [1.18.0] This determination of the rules of conduct has been stated in brief;
now hear this regarding disputes arising from purchase and sale.
[1.18.1 Commodity] Two types of property are declared: movable and immovable.
At the time of purchase, the term "commodity" (*paṇya*) is traditionally applied to both.
[1.18.2 Punishment for Buying Defective Goods] If an unwise person, knowing that a commodity is defective, sells it,
he shall be made to pay twice its value, as well as an equal amount as a fine.
[1.18.3 Things to be Relinquished] That which was sold by one who is intoxicated or insane, or for a low price out of fear,
or by one who is not independent or deluded, must be relinquished; it shall revert to him once again.
But he who, having sold an item into the hand of one person, delivers it to another, shall be made to pay double that value as a fine; the penalty for the offense shall be exactly that much.

[1.18.4 Times for Examination] The examination of seeds, base metals, draught animals, gems, women, milch cattle, and men shall take ten days, one day, five days, seven days, one month, three days, or half a month respectively.
If, however, a defect in the merchandise should arise before that time,
it must be returned by the seller, and the buyer shall recover the price.

But if something purchased is later discovered to be defective because it was bought without prior inspection, that merchandise must be returned to the owner at the proper time; otherwise, it need not be returned.
He should personally examine the merchandise and show it to others;
having accepted what has been examined and deemed satisfactory, he should not reject it again.
For horses, silver, gold, grain, iron, goats, and clothing,
as well as for products made of leather and wood, the period of examination shall be one day.
The valuation of pearls, elephants, horses, and slave-girls shall be determined by experts;
that of goods situated in the marketplace by the king’s command; and that of cattle and land by the mutual agreement of both parties.
In the case of sharing or exchange between both fields,
success in the task shall be achieved by those two through mutual recollection.
If those standing nearby—such as the relatives of the purchaser—are recorded [as witnesses], they should be questioned;
otherwise, if the transaction was conducted differently, one should then show the will of the relatives.
The purchase of immovable property is required to be based precisely on the testimony of relatives and others;
otherwise, if a purchase should take place, [the validity] shall be examined after three fortnights in another village.

Those born of the same womb, those connected by the offering of funeral cakes (sapinda), those connected by the offering of water (sodaka), those of the same lineage (gotra), neighbors, and creditors— these seven are considered sources from whom [a debt] may be recovered.
If one pays more or less than the price, it is considered improper regarding the value;
however, once the purchase is finalized, it shall not be rescinded even after hundreds of years.

[1.18.5 Special Rules for the Purchase of Land] Bṛhaspati states that in all sales, one should have recorded in writing wells, trees, and so forth, as well as water channels and whatever else exists, including other features.
They say that a field and so forth endowed with [favorable] qualities, ripened crops, a tree, or even fruit fit for enjoyment;
a well, a pond, a house, and high ground—these belong to the buyer and the seller alike.
If an exchange has been made by those who are intoxicated, deluded, ignorant, distressed, or confused,
or if it is at an improper price, the king shall annul all such transactions.
Relatives, neighbors, and creditors who have gone outside the village for the purpose of a purchase do not deserve to object [to the sale] once three fortnights have passed in succession.
Or else, after three fortnights, or a month, or after three months, he shall obtain that [result].
[1.19 Boundary Disputes] This rule has been set forth regarding rescission in the sale and purchase of villages,
fields, houses, and so forth; now learn the procedure for boundary disputes.

[1.19.1 Boundary Junctions: Trees and Other Markers to be Established] They should establish boundary trees— *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, *kiṃśuka*, *śālmalī*, *śāla*, and *tāla*— at the junctions of the boundaries.
And also milky trees.
Thickets, various kinds of bamboos, *śamī* trees, creepers, and mounds,
as well as reeds and thickets of *kubjaka*— by these, the boundary is not lost.
Reservoirs, wells, ...
and springs should be constructed at the junctions of boundaries, as well as temples for the deities.

Having granted a field, the king should cause it to be demarcated by the four classes of experts, the merchants, the water-officers, the inhabitants of the entire village, and the officials appointed by the lord of that larger territory.

BP1.19.006a. If a Śūdra should be the leader, one shall adorn him with the ornaments of eunuchs, smear his face with the ashes of a corpse, make five finger-marks on his chest with the blood of an animal sacrificed to Agni, fasten intestines around his neck, and have him carry a clod of earth from the boundary upon his head with his left hand.
At the time of settling [the land], the determination of the boundary must be made;
marked by both public and secret signs, it shall remove all doubt.
Imperishable goods, by their very nature, are not subject to conflict;
these include ponds, wells, tanks, sacred shrines, groves, and temples.
He should always cause these visible markers to be made for the boundary: high ground, depressions, river currents, reeds, thickets, mountains, and so forth.
[1.19.3 Witnesses in a Boundary Dispute] If there should be doubt even when signs are observed,
the determination of the boundary in a dispute must depend solely upon the testimony of witnesses.
In the absence of witnesses, four inhabitants living near the village boundaries shall,
being purified, determine the boundary in the presence of the king.

But in the absence of neighboring villagers who are original witnesses to the boundary, he should also interrogate these men who frequent the forests: BP1.19.012b/ imān api (anuyuñjīta puruṣān vana.gocarān //
Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers,
snake-catchers, gleaners, and others who dwell in the forest.
When they have been questioned, whatever mark they may declare at the junctions of the boundaries,
the king shall establish that accordingly for the two villages in accordance with the law.
Holding the earth upon their heads, wearing garlands and red garments,
and sworn by their respective good deeds, they shall speak the truth.
He should thus fix the boundary and record all those [markers] by name;
he should always cause these visible signs to be established at the boundary.
Likewise, he should establish other hidden marks which the earth would not consume,
and he should cause other boundary markers to be made that serve as protective coverings.
Upon perceiving the constant flux in the world regarding the knowledge of boundaries—
such as the bones in cemeteries, cow-hair ropes, ashes, and skull fragments— [one should understand the nature of existence].
He should cause cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel,
and likewise sand to be placed at the junctions of the boundary so that they remain hidden from view.
Cow-dung, bones, husks, charcoal, gravel, pebbles,
potsherds, sand, bricks, cow-hair, cotton-seeds, and ashes.
Having placed these [objects] in jars, he should have them deposited at the boundaries; these marks should be displayed with great care.
Then, he should diligently show them to children of tender age.
And in old age, they should likewise show those children [the boundary];
thus, when there is knowledge passed down through successive generations, no confusion regarding the boundary arises.
By the power of fortune or misfortune, he effects the taking away or the giving of men's possessions;
in one place there is the collapse of the earth's banks, while in another there is stability.
One should not displace the boundary that has been established along the bank of a river;
for when the land becomes desirable, it may overstep the field while still containing standing crops.
The owner of a field shall recover that land which has been seized by the king through anger or greed, by force or by legal decree, as it was carried away by the current of a river's flow.
[1.19.6 Decision on Disputes Concerning Houses and Fields] In disputes concerning houses and fields, the decision is reached based on the testimony of the neighbors,
as well as those who are the heads of city or village corporations and those men who are the most venerable.
Plowmen, artisans, laborers, cowherds, hunters, those who live by gleaning,
root-diggers, fishermen, and those who breach or obstruct irrigation channels;
Those who know the title-deed, the legal proof, the possession, the desire, the name,
and the characteristics of the portion of land— they are the witnesses in this matter.
But that land which was given by one who was pleased to another shall not attain validity if it was seized by the king through anger, greed, fraud, or even by legal means;
for such is the case when one enjoys land that lacks a valid title and was taken from someone else.
Or if she has been given to one superior in qualities, he must never cause her to be taken away from him.
Bound by their respective oaths, they shall declare the decision regarding the boundary;
they shall point out hidden deposits, for that is the established rule of evidence.
One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by the truth, and a Kṣatriya by his vehicles and weapons.
Even a single honest man, approved by both parties, who is free from identifying marks [of caste],
wearing red garlands and garments, and having taken earth upon his head, [may administer the oath].
A man, observing the vow of truth and fasting, shall point out the boundary.
If the neighbors should speak falsely when men are disputing over a boundary marker,
they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement.
Those who lead the case according to what has been stated are purified as truthful witnesses;
but those who lead it otherwise shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
This rule is proclaimed for every dispute concerning immovable property.
Those born there who reside in neighboring regions or other lands are designated as *maula* (original inhabitants); they should be questioned for the determination of legal cases.
Whatever those who are blameless, impartial, and of equal conduct may say when a doubt exists, that must be accepted as authoritative; in this way, dharma is not lost.
When land is brought from another village and given to someone else, it becomes the property of men in that manner; otherwise, any acquisition [of land] would be due to the king or fate.
Now, how is the legal determination made there by a king regarding a great river?
Land that is set aside by a river or granted by a king belongs to him alone;
otherwise, the acquisition of land by men would depend solely on fate or royal whim.
The decline, prosperity, and livelihood of men are subject to fate and the power of kings;
therefore, at all times, one should not subvert what has been ordained by them.
Where a river has been established as the boundary between two villages,
it may, by the power of fortune or misfortune of men, effect the loss or gain [of land];
and when, through its decrease or increase, it becomes small and shifts [the boundary], the king deserves to impose a fine.
The king should establish a clearly defined boundary for villages consisting of ten, a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand, using various distinctive marks.
Starting from the time of its construction, one must not displace a house, a garden, a shop, or any such property from its current state,
nor change its extent or the manner in which it was used by its owner.
One should not disturb the windows, the drainage channels, the turrets, the altars, or the water-channels of the quadrangular courtyard, provided they are situated toward the east.
One should not obstruct the girdle, the drainage channel, the eaves, or the windows;
by damaging a water-conduit or the site of a house, one shall be liable to pay a fine.

After the time of settling into a residence, these [prohibitions] should not be applied in any way whatsoever. One should not direct the gaze toward, nor construct a water-channel into, another person's house.
A latrine, a fire-pit,
a pit, or the place for pouring away water from food remnants should never be made too close to the wall of another's property.
One should construct receptacles for excrement, urine, and water, as well as a fire-place and a pit,
leaving a space of two *aratnis* from the front wall.
That by which people and animals go and come without being obstructed is called the cycle of existence (*saṃsaraṇa*); it must not be blocked by anyone.
If anyone there should out of desire create a mixture of castes, dig a pit, plant trees, or void excrement, his fine shall be one māṣaka.
Having taken [the draft animals], he should employ them at the proper time for sowing, guarding, and gathering;
if he fails to do so, he shall be made to pay the owner half of the harvested crop.
If anyone, having taken a field, neither cultivates it nor causes it to be cultivated,
he shall be made to pay the crop-rent to the owner and a fine equal to that amount to the king.
If the field has been neglected for a long time, one-tenth [of the produce] is due; likewise, if it is being cultivated, one-eighth;
but if it is well-prepared, one-sixth shall be assigned according to the rule.
[1.20 Harsh Speech] Harsh speech is traditionally held to be twofold: unpleasant verbal expression and physical assault.
Each of these is further divided into three types, and self-restraint is likewise said to have three characteristics.
[1.20.1 Regarding the three types of verbal abuse: Insulting the local customs, family lineages, and so forth, or joining them with evil— this,
when done without the use of physical force, is called the first type of verbal abuse.
The verbal abuse of one's sister or brother, as well as the reporting of their minor offenses (upapātaka),
is declared by those learned in the scriptures to be "middling" verbal violence.
The discourse on forbidden foods and drinks, the defilement by mortal sins, harshness of speech declared as the highest [offense], and the violent striking down of one who is defenseless;
[1.20.2 Punishment] But in the case of verbal abuse between those of equal caste and equal qualities,
the discipline prescribed in the treatise is a fine of twelve and a half panas.
A fine of two *kārṣāpaṇas* shall be imposed on those who are one-eyed, lame, or otherwise similarly disabled.
For insulting someone of equal caste, the fine is twelve *paṇas* and a half.
For insulting someone of lower caste, the fine is six *paṇas* and one *kākiṇī*.
The same applies to those who are one-eyed, lame, or otherwise disabled.

In cases of verbal abuse between equals, the punishment shall be equal; for an inferior, it shall be double; and for a superior, it is declared to be greater. Regarding mutual verbal abuse: BP1.20.008a/ [The same applies to] the one-eyed, the lame, and so forth. BP1.20.008b/ Between equals, the punishment is equal; for an inferior, it is double. BP1.20.008c/ For a superior, it is declared to be greater in cases of mutual verbal abuse.
If one insults a sister or other female relatives, he shall be fined fifty paṇas;
however, a Brāhmaṇa shall not be held liable for verbal abuse directed at those inferior in qualities.
Having declared an outcast to be an outcast, or a thief to be a thief,
one incurs an equal degree of guilt by such speech.
[1.20.3 Differentiation of Punishment according to Caste] If he imparts instruction on dharma to Brāhmaṇas in a manner contrary to dharma,
the king shall cause boiling oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears.
If a Kṣatriya brings false accusations against a Brāhmaṇa, his fine shall be fifty;
for a Vaiśya, it is twenty-five; and for a Śūdra, it is twelve and a half.
This discipline has been prescribed for a Śūdra who is virtuous and free from fault;
however, a Brāhmaṇa shall not incur guilt by using harsh words toward one who is devoid of good qualities.
A Vaiśya who reviles a Kṣatriya should be fined one hundred;
a Kṣatriya who insults a Vaiśya deserves half that fine as a disciplinary measure.
For insulting a Kṣatriya, a Śūdra shall be fined twenty-five paṇas;
for doing so to one of high rank, double that amount has been declared by those learned in the scriptures.
A Śūdra who insults a Vaiśya shall be made to pay the first amercement; for insulting a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement; and for insulting a Brāhmaṇa, the highest amercement.
One who defames another regarding their country and so forth shall be made to pay twelve and a half paṇas;
one who, out of arrogance, joins the other with a charge of sin shall be made to pay the first amercement.
One who provides instruction on the Dharma accompanied by citations from the Vedas,
but who reviles Brahmins, shall be punished by the cutting off of his tongue.
This punishment has been fully declared by me with reference to the status of the individual;
it should be determined by the wise according to whether the offense is equal, lesser, or greater.
[1.21 Cruelty with a Staff] [1.21.0] Assault with a staff is said to be the striking with hands, stones, or clubs; with ashes, mud, or dust; or with weapons and missiles.
When verbal abuse has been committed, whatever punishment is prescribed for the one who initiated it,
the king shall cause that very same person to pay double that fine, except in cases involving death.
When two persons strike each other, the punishment is declared to be equal for both;
however, the one who initiated the attack and the one who persisted in it shall be made to pay a higher fine.
A man who returns an insult for a previous insult, or strikes back when struck,
or even kills an assailant, incurs no guilt.
If a low-born person should insult a superior person with verbal abuse or other such acts, the king need not investigate that person when he strikes back in self-defense.
[1.21.1 First: Verbal Assault] The throwing of ashes and the like, as well as striking with the hand or other means, constitutes the first form of physical assault;
in this case, a fine of one *māṣa* shall be imposed.
This punishment has been declared for [intercourse with] women of equal status and those of higher status;
it should be understood by the wise as being double or triple, depending on the relative preeminence [of the woman].
For throwing stones, rocks, or wood, the first amercement shall be imposed;
likewise, for striking one another with hands or feet, the fine shall be ten and twenty paṇas respectively.
[1.21.2 Middle] When two parties have become agitated, the middle course should be employed in the application of force; however,
when an attack has actually occurred, the wise should impose a punishment proportionate to the deed committed at the time of the seizure.
For striking with a clod of earth, a stone, or a piece of wood, the fine shall be two māṣas;
for drawing blood, the punishment must be doubled by the wise.
For piercing the skin, the first amercement is the punishment; for piercing the flesh, however, the middle amercement;
for piercing a bone, the highest amercement shall apply, but for destroying [the bone], there shall be execution.
For cutting off the ears, nose, or hands; for breaking teeth;
or for piercing bones, the middle amercement shall be imposed; however, it shall be double in the case of those who have fallen from their caste.
For the cutting off of the ears, lips, nose, feet, eyes, tongue, penis, or hand, the highest fine is prescribed; for the piercing or mutilating of these, the middle fine is the rule.
The punishment for one who merely threatens is that prescribed for verbal assault;
if [the object] is actually taken, it is double that, and the royal fine is even greater than that.
In cases of piercing a limb, causing pain, or likewise inflicting a wound,
the offender shall be made to pay the expenses for recovery as well as whatever was seized during the quarrel.
But when one who was beaten in a secluded place is seen dead or appears to have been killed,
the killer should be identified either by inference or by an oath.
Where blood is seen in an inner apartment or in the forest at night where [the victim] was beaten, one should not question witnesses there.
If someone, having marked himself, should attack another out of malice for the sake of a pretext by means of excessive force, an investigation is appropriate in that case.
A man who, when reviled, reviles in return; or when struck, strikes back;
or who kills one who has committed an offense, shall not himself become an offender.
Likewise, those born in the inverse order (prātilomya) and the lowest castes are recorded as the impurities among men;
they are to be executed for violating a Brāhmaṇa, and their property must never be confiscated.
He who causes oxen that are exhausted, afflicted by hunger, or thirsty to work at an improper time shall be made to perform the expiation for killing a cow, or else he shall be made to pay a fine.
He shall be made to pay for the expenses incurred in recovering him and whatever was spent on the quarrel.
If a Śūdra strikes members of the twice-born classes in anger with any particular limb, that very limb of his shall be cut off; so it has been declared by Manu.
[1.22 Theft] [1.22.0] Thieves are recorded as being of two kinds: open and secret.
Through their wisdom, skill, and means, they are divided in a thousand ways.

[1.22.1 Thieves by Light and Darkness] Traders, physicians, gamblers, members of an assembly who take bribes, deceivers, those who predict omens and portents, auspicious men, artisans, and counterfeiters;
Those who fail to perform their duties, those who remain indifferent, and false witnesses— these are indeed open thieves, as are those who live by deceit.
Those who break into houses, those who rob travelers, those who carry off bipeds and quadrupeds, those who dig up crops, and those who steal grain are to be known as concealed thieves.
[1.22.2 Their Punishment] Those identified by royal officers through their associations, marks,
or appearances shall be made to restore what was stolen and be punished with penalties prescribed by the scriptures.
But the one who causes a breach [of the city wall] should be torn apart with pincers by the king’s officers;
the stealer of grain should be made to pay ten times [the value], and double the fine as well.
When the death of a single evildoer brings security to many, his execution bestows merit.
Likewise, one should hang a traveler from a tree at dawn by tying him by the neck.
For one who breaks a finger-joint, [the king] shall cause [the offending joint] to be cut off upon the first apprehension;
on the second, both hands and feet; on the third, he deserves the death penalty.
But a physician who is ignorant of medicinal herbs and mantras, and who does not understand the true nature of a disease,
yet takes wealth from the sick, shall be punished like a thief.
The stake must be made public; those who play with fraudulent dice shall be banished.
Those who play with false dice, the base, those who seize the wives of kings, accountants, and deceivers— these gamblers are declared to be punishable by law.
Furthermore, one who sells refined goods that are mixed with those of concealed defects shall be made to pay double the value of that merchandise, as well as a merchant's fine equal to that amount.
Those members of the court who speak unjustly, as well as those who live by bribery and those who deceive the trusting—
all of them shall be banished.
Those who, out of greed for wealth, proclaim to people knowledge of astrology and portents without actually understanding them, should be restrained with great effort.
Those who display themselves as being endowed with staffs, antelope skins, and other such emblems,
while secretly harming men through deception, shall be put to death by the king's officers.
Those who, by refining items of little value, bring them to a state of high value,
and those who deceive women and children, shall be punished in accordance with the nature of the offense.
Those who manufacture artificial gold, pearls, coral, and the like,
shall be made by the king to pay the value to the purchaser and a fine double that amount.
When neutral witnesses deceive one party through affection, greed, or other such motives,
and they give testimony otherwise than the truth, they shall be made to pay double the fine.
Those who, by the power of mantras or medicinal herbs, display some form of delusion or perform the rite of the "root" (*mūlakarman*), shall be banished by the king.
Those who break a boundary-mark, those who steal, and those who abandon [their kin] should be impaled on a stake;
likewise, a traveler who steals at dawn should be bound by the neck to a tree and suspended.

Those who carry off human beings should be burned by the king with a fire of straw; the stealer of a cow, however, the king shall have his nose cut off, or, having bound him, he shall drown him in water.
For stealing more than ten *kumbhas* of grain, the punishment is death;
for lesser amounts, he shall be made to pay eleven times the value, as well as the actual property to its owner.
A stealer of grain should be made to pay ten times its value, and double that amount as a fine.
Whether it be grass, or wood, or a flower, or a fruit—
one who takes these without having asked permission deserves the amputation of the hand.
One who has been well-conducted but becomes a thief shall suffer long in prison;
he must be made to restore that wealth to its owner, but no penance is to be performed for him.
[1.23 Sāhasa] [1.23.0 Sāhasa] This has been declared as the suppression of punishment for all types of thieves.
Now, let the legal procedure for the punishment of capital offenses in cases of violence be heard correctly.
Killing a human being, theft, violating another's wife,
and both forms of verbal and physical abuse constitute the fourfold category of *sāhasa* (heinous crimes).
That [fine] is proclaimed to be of three kinds—low, middling, and high—according to the nature of the object;
among them, the first, highest, and middle [fines] are determined in relation to the value of the property.
The wise have declared that these practices are to be avoided in the Kali Yuga: the killing of an *ātatāyin* (an assassin) or the foremost of the twice-born by means of a righteous war.

One who destroys or steals the implements of a field, an irrigation embankment, or the roots, flowers, and fruits [of that field] shall be fined one hundred panas according to the gravity of the offense.
One who destroys livestock, clothing, food, drink,
or household utensils shall be made to pay for them like a thief, as well as a fine of two hundred panas.
In the case of women, men, gold, gems, the property of gods or Brahmins,
silk garments, and other articles of superior value, the fine shall be equal to their market price.
Alternatively, kings may determine a double fine in consideration of the status of the person;
or the killer should be executed to prevent a recurrence of the offense.
Sāhasa (violent crime) is declared to be fivefold; among these, killing is considered the most severe.
Those who commit such acts are not to be punished with fines for wealth, but must be executed with diligent effort.
Those who are open murderers as well as those who are assassins by stealth,
having been properly identified and having plundered wealth, shall be executed by various means of death.

[1.23.1 Punishment for the Violent] Whether for the sake of gaining allies or for the acquisition of wealth, a king who seeks the welfare of the world must not release violent offenders, who bring fear to all people.
If a king, out of greed or fear, does not punish those who act unjustly,
his kingdom becomes agitated and he is deprived of his sovereignty.
That man who, motivated by anger or other such causes, causes others to perish by means of confinement, fire, poison, or a weapon, is a perpetrator of violence (*sāhasika*).
[1.23.2 Determination of Group Assault] Where many people, filled with rage, strike at one person,
he who deals the blow to a vital organ is declared the slayer.
But he who strikes a vital organ among them shall be made to pay the fine as prescribed;
likewise the instigator, the accomplice, the one who points out the way,
the shelterer, the provider of weapons, and the provider of food for those engaged in illegal acts.
One who instructs on war, one who demonstrates its destruction, one who is indifferent, one who is engaged in the task, one who points out faults, and one who approves [of them].
[1.23.3 Killing an Assassin] One who kills an assassin shall never incur guilt;
by slaying one who approaches seeking his destruction, he does not commit an offense.
He who does not kill an *ātatāyin*— even one of superior status who is endowed with good conduct and Vedic study,
though deserving of death— shall obtain the fruit of an *aśvamedha* sacrifice.
If one kills an assailant who is born of noble family and devoted to Vedic study, by not killing him he would become a killer of an embryo;
by killing him, he does not become a killer of an embryo.
Now, let the nature of violence and theft arising from anger and greed be heard;
[this is the determination regarding the identification of a killer]: the smallness of the wound, the fact that it was not fatal, and the location on a vital organ, all with great care.
Having ascertained both his capability and his motive through various signs, one should win him over.
But where a person is seen killed and the killer is not seen,
he should be identified by the king through the pursuit of prior enmity.
But he among them who is the actual striker shall be made to pay the fine as prescribed;
the one who incites the act and the helper shall each receive half of that penalty.
The neighbors living opposite and those living next door, as well as his friends,
enemies, and kinsmen, should be questioned by the king’s officers using conciliation and other such means.
He should be identified by men through association with the wicked or by the presence of stolen goods; this has been declared as the method for determining the intent of murderers and thieves.
But he who, having been apprehended on suspicion, does not proceed with that matter, must be cleared by an oath; this rule applies in all cases.
One who is purified by ordeals shall be deemed pure; one who is not pure deserves death.
Through such restraint and favor, the king’s fame and righteousness increase.
[1.24 Adultery with Women] [1.24.0] Harshness is declared to be of two kinds, and violence has two characteristics;
know that adultery, the root of evil, is of three types.
Two [types of union] are produced through the influence of force, while the third arises from passion;
that, moreover, is said to be threefold: inferior, middling, and superior.
That which is done against her will— by one who is asleep, insane, or intoxicated,
or by one who is prattling in secret— that indeed is an act committed by force.
When a union is brought about by leading a woman into a house under a pretext, or by administering intoxicants or drugs,
they know that to be a marriage contracted through fraud (*upādhi*).
That which is produced by mutual passion of the eyes, by the dispatching of female messengers,
and by the desire for beauty and wealth, should be known as born of mutual affection.
Furthermore, that is said to be of three kinds: the first, the middling, and the highest.
Glancing with a sidelong look, smiling, and likewise sending a female messenger.
The first [type of theft] is recorded as the touching of ornaments and garments, or their collection.
The sending of perfumes and garlands, incense on the road, garments,
and private conversation— they know this to be the middling form of seduction (*saṅgraha*).
Sharing a bed and a seat, as well as playing, kissing, and embracing—
this is declared by those who know the scriptures to be the highest form of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual misconduct).
The sending of perfumes, garlands, incense, ornaments, and garments,
as well as the enticing with food and drink, is recorded as the middling form of seduction.
The sending of perfumes, garlands, fruits, wine, food, and clothing,
as well as private conversation, they know to be the middling form of seduction.
For all three of these [offenses], the first, middle, and highest forms of discipline should be prescribed; however, for one possessing greater wealth, a higher penalty should be imposed.
But a man who engages in conversation with another's wife in secret,
having been previously accused of such offenses, shall incur the first amercement.
If one desires the entire wealth of another who is his rival,
he should have that person's penis and testicles cut off and paraded around on a donkey.
But he who should desire [her] through deception, his punishment shall be the confiscation of all his property;
having branded him with the mark of a female organ, he should then be banished from the city.
A man who is led by force into an assembly hall that is inferior to his own status should be fined; however, if he enters one that is superior, he shall be put to death.
If a woman, having come to his house, entices him with touching and other such acts and desires him there, she shall be punished; for the man, half of that fine is prescribed.
Those whose noses, lips, or ears have been severed should be submerged in water after being whirled around,
or they should be devoured by dogs in a place where many people are gathered.
But she who has been enjoyed against her will must be kept confined in the house;
with soiled limbs, sleeping on the ground, and subsisting on nothing more than a morsel of food.
If she has had intercourse with a man of equal caste, he should cause her to perform an expiation consisting of either a *kṛcchra* or a *parāka* penance;
however, if she has been enjoyed by a man of lower caste, she should be abandoned or else put to death.
[1.25 Means of Conduct for Women and Men] [1.25.0] This rule regarding adultery and the nature of adultery has been stated; now hear from me as I speak the means of conduct for women and men.
A woman should be kept away from even the slightest opportunities for misconduct by her own kinsmen;
she must be protected day and night by her mother-in-law and other elder women.
But she who, while indulging her own desires, is not restrained out of affection,
will inevitably suffer later, just like a neglected disease.
[1.25.1 Duties of Fathers,

Husbands, and Sons] A father who does not give [his daughter in marriage] at the proper time, a husband who does not approach his wife during her season, and a son who does not provide for his mother— each of these is subject to punishment according to dharma as a transgressor of domestic law.
Where women are honored, there the deities rejoice; there prosperity, progeny, and purity flourish, and every ritual action becomes fruitful.

Women should be employed in income and expenditure, the preparation of food, the maintenance of household utensils, cleanliness, and the performance of fire-rites; this is declared to be the purification for women.
A wife should be honored by her husband with garments, ornaments, and food,
especially during festivals, as well as by her paternal kinsmen, brothers, fathers-in-law, and other relatives.
She who does not transgress against her husband through thought, word, or deed is united with him in the world of husbands; she is called "virtuous" by the righteous.
[1.25.2 Corruptions of Women] A woman should not live in another's house separated from her husband, father, or sons; especially through association with the wicked, she certainly incurs reproach.
Rising before [the elders], eating and serving food after them,
occupying a lower seat, and sleeping later— this is declared to be the duty of women.
Drinking, wandering about, sleeping during the day, idleness, and the corruption of women.
When her husband is distressed, she is distressed; when he is joyful, she is joyful; when he has gone abroad, she is soiled and emaciated;
and when he dies, she follows him in death—such a woman is to be known as a devoted wife (*pativratā*).
When the lord is away on a journey, she should not engage in personal adornment, nor witness dances, songs, social gatherings, or festivals, nor should she indulge in meat or liquor.
A wife is declared to be half of one's own body, sharing equally in the fruits of merit and demerit;
following her husband in life and in death, that virtuous woman exists for his welfare.
One who is devoted to vows and fasting, firmly established in celibacy,
and constantly intent on the gift of Dharma, shall go to heaven even if she is childless.
[1.25.3 Prohibition of Niyoga] Having prescribed *niyoga*, Manu himself prohibited it;
because of the decline of the age (*yuga-hrāsa*), this cannot be performed by anyone according to the rules.
In the Kṛta and Tretā ages, men were endowed with austerity and knowledge;
however, in the Dvāpara and Kali ages, a decline in the power of men has been ordained.
[1.26 Partition of the Inheritance] [1.26.0] That wealth which is given (or is being given) by the father to his sons is called *dāya* (inheritance). ... [text missing] ... //
One woman should be made to perform work in each house according to her share; many women may be assigned tasks with equal shares. This same rule applies even to male slaves.
Having drawn water from a well or a pond, it is taken according to the [established] order;
likewise, a field is divided by means of a boundary embankment according to the [fixed] proportion of shares.
That [property] must be divided according to reason; otherwise, it would be useless.

[1.26.1 Distinct Characteristics] For those living together with a single cooking fire, the worship of the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born should be performed collectively; however, for those who maintain separate fires, that same worship must be performed in each individual household.
Witnessing, acting as a guarantor, giving, and receiving—these brothers who have divided their inheritance may perform among themselves; those who have not divided may not.
Those among whom these transactions proceed in the world regarding their own inheritance,
one should recognize them as divided, even in the absence of a written document.
The obstruction of family lineage and the destruction of property, as well as the proof of a violent act,
constitute separate wealth from the partition of immovable property held for one's own enjoyment.
[1.26.2 The Time of Partition] The partition among brothers has been demonstrated to take place upon the death of both parents,
when the mother’s menses have ceased and her sisters have been given away in marriage.
[1.26.3 The Order of Partition] Regarding ancestral houses and fields that have come down by succession, the father and sons are entitled to equal shares; however,
they are not entitled to a partition of the paternal estate against the father's will.
Those sons of twice-born men who are born of wives of equal caste shall all divide the inheritance equally after giving a preferential share (*uddhāra*) to the eldest.
Indeed, by virtue of age, learning, and austerity, one receives two shares of the wealth;
for as the wealth obtained through partition is applied to the purpose of sacrifice,
so should the learned increase the weight of that share.
Their sons, whether equal or unequal [in number], are declared to be entitled to their father's share.
Regarding property acquired by the grandfather, whether it be immovable or movable,
equal ownership has indeed been declared for both the father and the son.
If shares that are equal, deficient, or excessive have been assigned by the father to his sons, they must be maintained exactly as they were; otherwise, they should be corrected.
But in the case of a division during the father's lifetime, the father shall take two shares for himself.
The division of inheritance for heirs is proclaimed to be of two kinds:
one according to the order of seniority by age, and the other an equal distribution of shares.
When property is acquired by those who have come together, all of them are entitled to equal shares therein;
it is recorded that their sons, whether unequal or equal [in number], shall inherit the father’s portion.
All sons who inherit their father's estate are entitled to equal shares;
however, among them, one who is devoted to learning and virtuous conduct deserves to receive more.
He whose fame in this world is celebrated for the sake of sacred learning, practical knowledge, and valor, and for acts of imparting wisdom, by him his ancestors have truly become possessed of a son.
The eldest, by virtue of birth, learning, and qualities, shall receive two shares of the inheritance;
the others, however, shall share equally, for he is equal to his father.
In the absence of that [father], however, the mother shall receive a share equal to her son's;
their other mothers shall receive equal shares, and the unmarried daughter shall receive a fourth of a share.
For unmarried daughters, however, one-fourth share is prescribed;
for sons, there are three shares. But equality is ordained when the wealth is small.
If there are many sons born of one [mother], equal in number according to their birth-order,
they shall divide the property belonging to that mother among themselves in accordance with the law.
Among those [wives] of the same caste who differ in number, the share of the male portion is recommended;
however, all those grandmothers on the mother's side are declared to be equal to mothers.

But those among them who have not been consecrated with sacraments should be consecrated by their elder brothers from the paternal wealth alone, just as the unmarried daughters are, according to the rule.
If there are brothers who have not received the sacraments,
those younger ones among them should be initiated by their elder brothers from the paternal wealth held in common.
And he should give him sufficient wealth or a share of the field, whichever he desires.
That which is received by a married woman or even by an unmarried daughter from her husband, from her father's house,
from her brother, or from her parents, is declared to be *saudāyika* (gift of affection).
Upon receiving a dowry, independence is prescribed for women,
because that was given by their [relatives] for the sake of compassion as a means of subsistence.

In the sale or even the gift of immovable property, the woman's wealth may be disposed of as she desires; however, it shall belong to her offspring, and the daughter is entitled to a share thereof. If she is unmarried, she receives that share; but if she is married, she receives only a token honorarium.
A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a paternal uncle’s wife,
a father’s sister, a mother-in-law, and the wife of an elder brother are declared to be equal to a mother.
If these women have neither a biological son nor a daughter's son,
their wealth shall go to their sister's sons, or those who are related through the female line.
[1.26.4 Characteristics of a Son] Even one born of a wife of the same caste is unworthy of the paternal wealth if he lacks good qualities; rather,
that [wealth] is ordained for those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) who offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) for him.
A son protects his father from those who are heavily indebted as well as from those who owe him a small debt;
therefore, there is no purpose served by one who acts in the opposite manner.
"What is the use of that cow which neither gives milk nor bears calves?
What is the purpose of a son being born who is neither learned nor righteous?"
A son who is devoid of learning, heroism, and wealth, lacking in austerity and wisdom,
and deficient in proper conduct, is declared to be equal to urine and excrement.
[1.26.5 Partition of Sons] Even immovable property and bipeds, though acquired by oneself,
may not be given away nor sold without having assembled all the sons.

Those humans who are already born, those yet to be born, those dwelling in the womb, and those residing in the world of the ancestors—all of them desire that livelihood; therefore, it must not be cut off.
Household utensils, vehicles, and the like, as well as food, ornaments, and servants, are divided while being visible; however, in the case of hidden property, the examination of hair is prescribed.
Those born of the Kṣatriya [caste] receive three, two, and one shares respectively; those born of the Vaiśya [caste], however, receive two and one shares.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras born from a Brāhmaṇa [father] in successive order shall possess four, three, two, and one shares respectively.
A son born of a Śūdra woman by men of the twice-born castes does not deserve a share of land; the twice-born man shall receive everything—thus the law is settled.
Among them, those sons who are of the same caste as their father shall receive a third share;
those of lower caste shall live with him, provided with food and clothing.
For all these sons of one who has no son of the body are declared to be heirs; however, once a son of the body is born, their status as the eldest ceases to exist.

That which has been given by the grandfather, the father, and that which may have been given by the mother—none of that should be taken away from him; likewise, so too his wealth acquired through valor and the wealth of his wife.
Those who stated that clothing and such items are indivisible have not reflected upon the fact that for the wealthy,
wealth consists primarily of clothes and ornaments.
A debt that has been recorded in writing and acknowledged... [rest of verse]
Indeed, when a debt is recorded on a document, it should be understood according to the manner described;
it must be divided by means of verbal testimony, for otherwise it would be meaningless.
If a property situated in the middle is such that it cannot be sustained by one person alone, it must be divided with due consideration; otherwise, it would be useless.
Having sold clothing and ornaments, or having received money for which a document was written,
or having exchanged prepared food for unprepared food, [the property] is divided.
The profit from property used for acquisition and preservation shall be divided equally; and the heirs must always manage its use according to their respective shares.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take the land that has become a religious endowment (*brahmadāya*);
likewise, all twice-born men shall take the house and the field that have come down by hereditary succession.
[1.26.6 The Arrangement for Those Divided with the Father] Those uterine brothers or half-brothers who have been divided from the father,
as well as those who are junior to them— they alone are entitled to receive the father’s share.
The elder brother born before partition has no authority over the paternal estate; the brother born after partition has no authority over the share of his brothers.

Whatever has been acquired by a father himself after he has divided his property with his sons, all that belongs to the son born after the partition; it is declared that the elder brothers have no right to it.
Just as with wealth, so too with debts, gifts, non-gifts, and purchases,
they have no mutual authority over one another, except regarding impurity and the water-libation rites.
Regarding property inherited from a grandfather that was seized by the father and subsequently acquired through his own power—
such as by means of learning, valor, or other such means— the father's ownership over it is declared in the legal tradition.
One may make a gift at one's own will, as well as an enjoyment from that wealth;
in the absence of such [a gift or enjoyment], the sons are declared to have equal shares.
Having honored with perfumes and garlands the father’s clothes, ornaments, bed, vehicle, and so forth, one should present them to the recipient of the *śrāddha* feast.
If ornaments have been worn by women while their husband is still living, the heirs shall not divide them; those who do divide them fall from their caste.

Through the father’s favor, garments and ornaments are enjoyed [by the sons]. Where an heir comes forward, whether the partition has been made or not, if he provides for what is common, he shall indeed receive a share.
If a man possesses a debt, a document, a house, or a field inherited from his grandfather,
he shall receive his share even if he has been away for a long time, provided he returns.
If one who shared in the ancestral estate abandons it and takes refuge in another country,
a share must undoubtedly be given to him upon his return from half the distance.
If the origin of births cannot be determined, one who is the third, fifth, or even the seventh [in descent] shall receive his share according to the order of succession.
If all the original hereditary tenants know a person to be their lord through a continuous line of succession,
then the land must be given to him when he arrives as a member of that lineage by his kinsmen.

For kinsmen who have lived together, whether they were previously undivided or subsequently divided, a further partition of the inheritance may take place up to the fourth generation; such is the settled rule.
[1.26.7 Varieties of Sons] Sons have been classified in many ways by the ancient seers;
they cannot be established now by those who lack the power and are long past their prime.
The legitimate son of the body alone is declared the sole owner of the paternal estate;
the son of an appointed daughter is equal to him, while all others are recorded as being entitled only to maintenance.
But the other sons, beginning with the son begotten on the wife (kṣetraja), are entitled to five, six, or seven shares.
The *datta* (given), the *apaviddha* (cast off), the *krīta* (bought), the *kṛta* (made), and likewise the *śaudra* (born of a Śūdra woman)—
these, being pure by birth, are all recorded as middle sons who share in the inheritance.

The son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), as well as the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the maiden-born son (*kānīna*), the son received with the bride (*sahoḍha*), the son born in secret (*gūḍhaja*), and the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-suta*) are despised by the virtuous.
The son of a Śūdra woman, one who has given himself, and those who are known as "purchased"—all these are declared to be Maitras; they are undoubtedly Kāṇḍapṛṣṭhas.
He who, having cast his own family behind him, goes instead to the family of another—
by that misconduct he is undoubtedly a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*.
Gautama said that [the rite] is performed after sacrificing to Agni and Prajāpati;
however, others say that for one who has no son, a daughter may be designated as a son (putrikā) with due reflection.
Thirteen types of sons were previously declared by Manu;
among them, the son of the body (aurasa) and the appointed daughter (putrikā) are the causes for the continuation of the lineage.
Just as oil is remembered by the wise as a substitute for clarified butter when the latter is unavailable,
so too are the eleven types of sons considered substitutes for the appointed daughter and the legitimate son of the body.
If there are many uterine brothers born of the same father,
it is traditionally held that when a son is born to even one of them, they are all considered to have sons.
This same rule is prescribed for many wives who have a single husband;
if one among them has sons, he alone is the giver of the rice-balls for all of them.
Since a son saves his father from the hell named Put,
he should strive for the birth of such a son even by merely looking upon his face.
Both the grandson and the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) cause one to attain heaven;
they are declared to be equal in regard to both the inheritance of property and the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
And if the son born of a Śūdra woman from a marriage out of lust remains obedient, his brothers shall give him a mere token of respect as his share when their father has died.
For the sake of food, one *prastha* of rice along with fuel should be provided in the afternoon;
furthermore, a garment purchased for three *paṇas* should be given once every three months.
[1.26.8 The Widow’s Share] Only this much has been prescribed as the wealth for a virtuous widow.
Having set aside the value of the clothing, the food, and likewise that of the washerman, one should assign the remainder to those entitled to the inheritance.
Now, for one who has no son, the wife born of a family of equal status, or the daughters, are entitled;
in their absence, the father, the mother, the brother, and the sons are declared [to be the heirs].
A man without a son should, with great effort, adopt a son of whatever kind may be available,
for the sake of performing the offering of funeral cakes and water, and for the proclamation of his religious merit.
The ancestors, fearing the descent into hell, long for sons, thinking: "Whoever shall go to Gayā will deliver us."
Just as a man drowning while crossing water with a leaky boat sinks down,
even so a father sinks into blinding darkness because of a bad son.
"He will perform the ritual release of a bull, as well as sacrifices and works of public utility;
he will protect the kingdom in his regency and offer ancestral oblations every day."
[1.26.9 Wife as a Share] According to the Vedas, the treatises of tradition, and the conduct of the world,
the wise have declared that a wife is half of one's body, sharing equally in the fruits of both merit and demerit.
He whose wife has not passed away lives with half of his body;
while half of the body still lives, how could another take possession of that wealth?
But when agnates— namely, paternal uncles and blood relations— are present,
the wife of a deceased man who leaves no son shall take his share.
When the husband has died, the wife devoted to her husband shall inherit his wealth, including the Agnihotra fire that was previously maintained; this is the eternal law.
A woman who has died [unwidowed] shall take the *mūrva* grass; one who has ascended the funeral pyre with her husband shall take the sin.
In the absence of a son, the wife shall be the heir; in the absence of a wife, the uterine brother; in his absence, the heir; and after that, the daughter's son shall inherit the wealth.
Having taken moving and stationary property, gold, silver, grain, liquids, and clothing, one should cause the Śrāddha for the monthly, six-monthly, and other occasions to be performed.

One should honor with offerings for the ancestors (*kavya*) and for the gods (*pūrta*) one's paternal uncles, teachers, daughters' sons, sisters' husbands, and maternal uncles; as well as the elderly, guests, and women.
Whatever rules regarding mortgages and the like are prescribed concerning divided property,
a wife whose husband has passed away may receive that, with the exception of immovable property.
Even if she has been established in her duties and a share has already been assigned, a woman does not have a right to immovable property.
If a widow, being in the prime of youth, becomes harsh,
then a livelihood must be provided for the purpose of sustaining her life.
When her husband has died, a woman who protects the family shall receive her husband’s share;
for as long as she lives, her ownership over it is restricted, and she may not give, mortgage, or sell it.
A woman who has been purchased by purchase, or one taken for the sake of sexual enjoyment by a man desiring offspring— even if she belongs to another— is indeed declared to be a wife.
He should indeed give either a funeral cake or a share of the field according to his own will.
Whatever property for subsistence has been given by a father-in-law to women from immovable assets cannot be taken away by others after the father-in-law has died.
Those sapindas or kinsmen who act as obstacles to her [the woman] and would seize her property— the king shall have them executed with the punishment prescribed for a thief.
[1.26.10 Division of Re-united Property] Furthermore, two who have reunited out of affection shall share in each other's property;
likewise, brothers who, having been divided, live together again in one place out of mutual affection.
If there is a subsequent division of property among them, their seniority no longer exists.
If he should at any time die or somehow renounce the world, his share is not lost; it is ordained for his uterine brother.
His sister, however, deserves to receive a share from that [inheritance];
this is the law for one who is childless and lacks both a wife and a father.
Whether she has been given away or not given away, if a uterine brother dies, she alone shall take his share;
for this is clearly the reason for both cases.
The wealth of each person shall belong to his nearest sapinda relative.
If one has died without offspring, without a wife, and without brothers, father, or mother,
all his *sapiṇḍa* relatives shall divide that inheritance according to their respective shares.
Among those who have reunited, if any one of them acquires wealth through learning, valor, or other such means,
two shares of that wealth shall be given to him, and the remainder shall share it equally.
Furthermore, one who was previously divided but has lived together again with his father, brother,
or paternal uncle out of affection is called "reunited" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*).
The uterine brothers, having assembled together in union, shall divide that [property] equally,
as shall the brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters.
If among them the eldest or the youngest is excluded from the distribution of shares,
or if either of them dies, his share is not lost.
But a uterine brother [shall give and take] the share of a uterine brother, whether he is born or deceased.
But a uterine brother who is a co-resident shall not take the wealth from one who is not uterine;
and even if he is not a co-resident, a uterine brother shall give [the share], but not one born of a different mother.
But for those whose fathers are deceased, the allotment of shares is calculated from the father's side.
Those Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are childless and deprived of wives and brothers—
the king shall take their wealth, for he is the sovereign lord of all.
[1.26.11 Distinction among sons according to their caste] A son born of a Kṣatriya woman by a Brāhmaṇa, being the eldest by birth and endowed with good qualities,
shall receive an equal share with the Kṣatriya son; and likewise, a son born of a Vaiśya woman [by a Brāhmaṇa].

Land received as a gift should never be given to a son of a Kṣatriya or other such caste, even if their father might have given it; however, upon the death [of the father], the son of a Brāhmaṇa may take it.
One born of a Śūdra woman by men of the twice-born castes does not deserve a share of land; he shall receive everything from his own [step-]brother—thus the law is settled.
If a Niṣāda is the only son of a Brāhmaṇa, he shall receive one-third of the estate;
the two remaining shares shall be taken by kinsmen (sakulyas) or sapindas who offer the funeral oblations (svadhā).
In the absence of kinsmen, the giver of the *svadhā*— whether it be the teacher or even the pupil—
should likewise provide for those castes in all calamities.
A virtuous son born of a Śūdra womb who serves a childless man shall receive enough for his livelihood;
the remainder of the estate the sapinda relatives shall obtain.
The wife is the heir to her husband's wealth; in her absence, the daughter is declared [the heir].
"A daughter arises from every limb of men, just like a son;
therefore, how could another man take the father's wealth?"
In the absence of those [heirs], however, if there is an unmarried daughter, then, in the absence of sons or grandsons, the daughters' sons shall obtain the wealth.
For just as one's own self, so is a son; and by means of a son, a daughter is equal [to a son].
Since they reside within that very self, how could anyone else take away the wealth?
"In this world, according to the law, there is no difference between a grandson and a daughter's son;
by this very ordinance, he then made his daughter a *putrikā* (an appointed daughter)."
A male is produced when the male seed is in excess; a female is produced when the female seed is in excess.
A wife who is equal [in status], wedded by an equal, virtuous, and devoted to service—
whether she has borne children or not— is the heir to her father’s wealth through her son.
Just as she has ownership over her father’s property even while her kinsmen are present,
so too does her son have a right to the desired wealth of his mother and maternal grandfather.
In the absence of those, however, the brothers, the sons of brothers, the uterine kinsmen,
the distant relatives, the paternal kinsmen, the disciples, and those learned in the Vedas are entitled to the wealth.
[1.26.13 Division of the Estate of One Without Sons] The mother shall inherit the estate of a son who dies childless; indeed,
she shall inherit the estate of a son who dies destitute of both wife and children.
The mother should be known as the heir to the inheritance, or the brother with her permission.
In the absence of a son, however, the wife shall [inherit]; in the absence of the wife, the uterine brother;
in his absence, the heir; and after that, the daughter's son shall take the wealth.
From the wealth that has been acquired, he should diligently set aside half for that purpose,
specifically for the monthly, six-monthly, or annual *śrāddha* ceremonies.
Where there are many kinsmen, such as *sakulyas* and *bāndhavas*,
he who is the nearest among them shall take the wealth of one who leaves no offspring.
A brother, or a brother’s son, or a sapinda, or even a disciple,
having performed the piṇḍa-rite together, should thereafter perform the rite for prosperity.
If one who has made a partition by his own will should again act inconsistently with it, he shall be compelled by the king to abide by his own share and punished for his misconduct.
In cases of denial regarding a joint debt or a deposit,
or when one has committed a fraudulent act that causes loss to another's side, the judge shall not compel payment by force.
Those men who are deceitful, possessors of wealth, cruel,
and greedy should be won over through affection, or else by the loss of their own interests and through stratagem.
Violence, ownership of immovable property, and the prior partition among heirs are to be known through inference when there are no witnesses present.
These activities of theirs proceed in the world among their own heirs;
one may recognize them as divided even without a written document.
Those who have not divided their inheritance must perform the Vaiśvadeva and other such rites together.
The obstruction of force and its persistence, the seizure of property, and the intent for violence; the enjoyment of one's own immovable property, and separate wealth from the partition.
Those who maintain separate incomes, expenditures, and assets, and engage with one another in lending,
trade, and commerce, have undoubtedly divided their property.
When brothers have divided their property among themselves, they should mutually record the transaction in writing with a public proclamation;
or, when dividing it, they may appoint blameless witnesses to prevent future disputes.
Whatever share of whatever kind has been enjoyed by whom, that one shall not be deprived of it.

[1.27 Gambling] [1.27.0] Gambling, which destroys truth, purity, and wealth, was forbidden by Manu; however, when it is conducted by others [as a regulated sport], it is accompanied by a share for the king.
The proceedings presided over by the master of the gambling house are for the purpose of identifying thieves;
this same rule is to be understood as applicable to animal-betting and to the game of dice.
[1.27.1 The Conduct of the Master of the Gaming Hall] The master of the gaming hall shall be the collector there; he shall pay [the winnings] to the victor and to the king.
From the gambling proceeds, a ten-percent royalty shall be paid to the king by the master of the gaming hall.
Or it may be according to the agreed time... [and so forth].
[1.27.2 Victory and Defeat of the Master] If anyone should suffer exhaustion in a duel,
the master must pay the wager that was stipulated for that occasion.

One who has been defeated in secret, or one who is ignorant of the game, or one who uses false dice or deceit, must be released—even if he is knowledgeable; furthermore, he shall not be made to pay the entire stake won.
[1.27.3 Punishment for fraudulent gambling] Those wicked gamblers who play with false dice, those who steal the king’s share,
and those who practice deception in counting, are declared by tradition to be punishable.
A public proclamation must be made:
"Those who practice fraudulent gambling shall be banished; however, one who commits such acts with intent to kill shall suffer various forms of capital punishment."
[1.27.4 Determining Victory and Defeat when Doubtful] That same witness, surrounded by three other members of the court (*sabhyas*), shall resolve the doubt between the two parties; however,
the gamblers themselves are the judges of the doubtful matter.
But when they become hostile, then the king should investigate.
In this manner, the king should daily examine the legal cases brought by litigants,
as well as other matters depending on the king, together with learned Brāhmaṇas.
[1.28 Gambling] [1.28.0] When birds, rams, bulls, and the like, having been mutually selected and staked upon, strike one another, they call that *samāhvaya* (gambling).
If anyone should suffer defeat in a duel,
his master must pay the wager that was stipulated for that occasion.
[1.29 Miscellaneous] This judicial procedure performed by litigants has been declared in brief; now I shall explain the miscellaneous judicial procedure based upon the king.
Having ascertained the nature and extent of the offender's fault, the king should impose one of the fourfold punishments— reprimand, fine, censure, or corporal punishment— as appropriate.
One who deserves the death penalty shall pay a fine of one hundred gold pieces;
for the amputation of a limb, half of that; and for exile, twenty-five.
The hands, feet, genitals, eyes, tongue, ears, and nose;
the tongue, half of the foot, the pincers (the thumb and index finger), the forehead, the lips, the anus, and the hips.
These fourteen locations for punishment have been specified;
however, for a Brāhmaṇa, branding on the forehead is ordained, and no other form of punishment is prescribed.
One should diligently restrain the unrighteous by three means:
by confinement, by imprisonment, and by various forms of intimidation.
But when one is unable to restrain these [enemies] even by means of piercing [them with weapons],
then one should employ all four of these methods against them.
One should first apply the punishment of verbal censure, immediately after that the punishment of reproach,
thirdly the punishment of a fine, and after that the punishment of corporal chastisement.
And he should place all prisons along the royal highway,
where those who have committed evil deeds may be seen suffering and disfigured.
He who cremates the corpse of one who has died without relatives shall take a tenth part of the wealth, or a fifth, or even the whole of it.
Tenth part for one who has many dependents to protect, and fifth part for one who has few;
Śaunaka says that for one whose father’s wife has no son, he may take the whole estate.
A sixth part [of the value] shall be paid as a ferry-toll when one has crossed; likewise, those who incite war, thieves, sowers of dissension, and those who destroy crops must pay the same.

A hidden treasure, the wealth of a family-less person, the arrival of fortune for a pauper,

The provocation of the constituent elements, mutual conspiracy,

In the case of the disqualification of witnesses, members of the court, or the parties themselves, there shall be a retrial;
